===== SECTION: Data and transmission rules =====

# Data and transmission rules

The people who hold language data decide how it is used. The rails write their
decisions beside each file, and every tool obeys what is written — with
community ownership and control of language data as the design rule, not a
setting. This page is the rule set, exactly: what each field does, what the
tools refuse, and the parts only you can keep.

## The sidecar (set/1)

Beside any data file, `<file>.champollion.json`, `$schema`
`https://champollion.dev/schemas/set/1.json`. Unknown keys are refused; notes
go under `x-`. A sidecar written before set/1 (no `$schema`) is read as set/0
and stays valid (`champollion upgrade` rewrites it).

| Field | Values | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `transmission` | `local-only` (the only value) | Only a model on this computer may see the text; every tool refuses to send it anywhere (`mt-eval project offer` included) |
| `role` | `train` · `dev` · `test` · `sealed` · `input` · `resource` | What the file is for. `test` and `sealed` are never trained on |
| `kind` | `parallel` · `monolingual` · `lexicon` · `grammar` · `glossary` | What it holds |
| `pair` | `{source, target}` | The direction its columns run, in the cards' codes |
| `fields` | `{source, target}` | Which column or JSON field holds which side |
| `terms.training` | `allowed` · `not-allowed` | `not-allowed`: no model may be trained on it |
| `terms.owner` | text | Who holds it, in the holder's words |
| `terms.speakers` | text | Whose words it holds, in the holder's words |
| `terms.speakers_agreed` | `yes` · `not-yet` · `some-said-no` | Whether the people whose words these are agreed |
| `terms.consent_record` | path | The consent note, relative to the file's folder |
| `holders_agreed` | `{by, date}` | Who among the holders agreed that a local-only output may sit where it is (loosens nothing) |
| `derived_from` | path | The protected file this one was made from; its marks were carried here |
| `id`, `name`, `license`, `tier`, `segment`, `sha256`, `rows`, `card`, `registeredAt` | | Written by `champollion network register-corpus`; a changed file (another sha256) no longer gets the card's id |
| `written_by` | text | The command that wrote it |

**Lock.** A sidecar only makes a file stricter: it never loosens what a corpus
envelope or a registry entry says.

## Local-only, and the provisional default

`champollion data add` marks the file it writes local-only when the project's
`defaults.transmission` is `local-only` (what `champollion new` writes), and
always for `--into test`. That mark is the tool's protection until the holders
answer, flagged `"x-transmission-default": true`.

- The holders' first answer decides. `champollion data mark <file>
  --may-leave` lifts a provisional mark; `--local-only` makes it theirs (the
  flag is removed).
- **Note.** The tool cannot tell who ran the command. Lift a provisional mark
  only with the holders' own answer.
- **Lock.** A local-only mark the holders made cannot be lifted by any
  command: *"this file is marked local-only, and a sidecar only ever gets
  stricter. Whether it may leave this computer is its holders' decision — if
  they agree, edit the sidecar by hand."*
- **Lock.** `data mark` on a file not yet local-only needs `--local-only` or
  `--may-leave`: *"whether this file's text may ever be sent to an outside AI
  service is its holders' decision, so it is never assumed"*.

What local-only means in each tool:

| Where | What happens |
|---|---|
| Any evaluation (`mt-eval run`, forge scoring) | The policy resolves to `sealed` (tier `local-only`): only a loopback endpoint, the harness's own in-process adapter (`local-model`), or an external method run with `--attest-local-transport` may see the text |
| Terminal and `--json` output | Its sentences are withheld; line numbers, ids, counts and scores are printed instead, with one line saying why |
| Files carved from it | Splits, cleaned copies, hypotheses and run logs keep the text (they are in the person's folders) and carry the mark in a sidecar of their own |
| A model trained on it | Its output is local-only too (`forge-model.json` `trained_on.terms`; unrecorded counts as local-only): `try_translation` returns only the model's page, `champollion connect`, `mt-eval serve` off loopback and `mt-eval translate` outside the project need `--holders-agreed-by`, and `sync` holds back its answers, through the `api` and the `local` method alike ([serving](/docs/agents/serving)) |
| A coaching file or dictionary | A coaching file with a sidecar carries its policy to the prompt; a lexicon run's outputs are withheld when its dictionary is local-only |

**Note.** `--attest-local-transport` declares a method's endpoint local. Pass
it only when you have verified the endpoint is on this machine: a loopback
address can be a proxy that forwards anywhere.

## Training

- **Lock.** nmt-forge refuses to train on a file whose sidecar says
  `terms.training: not-allowed`; an unreadable sidecar counts as a
  restriction, never as none.
- **Lock.** `champollion data combine` never joins a not-allowed file: it moves
  it, with its sidecar, to `data/not-for-training/`. It refuses a file whose
  holders have not answered yet — no `terms.training`, or no
  `terms.speakers_agreed` (*"nobody has said yet whether everyone whose words
  are in it agreed — champollion next asks the people; combine afterwards"*) —
  and the joined file carries the strictest of the files' terms (local-only if
  one is, not-allowed if one is, every owner named).
- **Lock.** The journey's terms step counts a file in `data/parallel/`,
  `data/lexicon/`, `data/grammar/` or `data/monolingual/` as answered only when
  its sidecar has both `terms.training` and `terms.speakers_agreed` (and the
  training answer is the holders', not the tool's caution below); until then
  it asks again, and the rails go no further.
- **Note.** nmt-forge reads `terms.training`, not `speakers_agreed`. With one
  pair file there is no combine, so only the terms step waits for that
  answer: never train a file whose speakers' answer is missing.
- **Lock.** A `test` or `sealed` file is never trained on: `--training
  allowed` is refused for it, and giving it another role is refused.
- **Lock.** `not-allowed` cannot become `allowed` by command (*"If its holders
  agree to training, edit the sidecar by hand"*) — with one exception below.
- Scripture (USFM) comes in with `terms.training: not-allowed` marked as the
  tool's caution (`"x-training-default": true`); the holders' answer replaces
  it.

## Whose words, and who agreed

`--speakers` records whose words the file holds; `--speakers-agreed` whether
they agreed.

| `speakers_agreed` | Effect |
|---|---|
| `yes` | Training as the holders said |
| `not-yet` | Training is forced to `not-allowed` until they all agree; the file appears in `waiting_for_agreement` |
| `some-said-no` | No model may learn from the file, ever: *"take their words out into another file, and mark the rest"* |
| (no answer) | The terms step keeps asking, and `data combine` refuses the file (above) |

**The one loosening a command makes:** `not-yet` → `yes` together with
`--training allowed`. A file `combine` had set aside then returns to
`data/parallel/` for the next combine.

**Note.** Ask the `waiting_for_agreement` question once a session, gently, and
answer it only with the person's yes that everyone agreed.

**`--holders-agreed-by "<who>"`** names a person among the data's holders who
agreed that a local-only output may go somewhere specific: into an app's locale
files (`champollion connect`, recorded as the pair's `holdersAgreed`), onto
an address other machines reach (`mt-eval serve`, `nmt-forge serve`, reported
on `/health`), or into a file outside the project (`mt-eval translate`,
recorded as the sidecar's `holders_agreed`). It loosens nothing else: the
output stays local-only for every tool. **Note.** Pass only the name the person
gave you.

## What tools print, and never print

| Tool | Prints | Never prints |
|---|---|---|
| `champollion data add` | Counts, columns (letter, fill rate, mean length, share of Latin letters), a header cell only when it names one of the pair's languages, ELAN tiers by number, and the row numbers its row check names | A sentence; any other header cell (its length instead); an ELAN tier's id |
| `champollion data mark`, `combine`, `next`, `validate` | Fields, counts, states | A data file's text — they never open it |
| `champollion improve …` | Counts and percentages | The sheets' sentences |
| `champollion sync` (the `local` and `api` methods) | The keys whose text holds words a forge model never saw in training, from the server's `meta.unseen_words` | The text, or the words themselves |
| `nmt-forge`, `mt-eval` | For a local-only, sealed or consent-required corpus: ids, line numbers, counts, scores; `[sentence withheld]` inside error messages | Its sentences, in human or `--json` output |
| MCP rails tools | What the CLI prints, trimmed | Sentences; the output of a local-only model |

**Note.** `--show-text` (nmt-forge; `mt-eval compare`) prints withheld
sentences. It is for a person at their own terminal, never for an agent —
what you read goes to your model provider.

**Note.** No tool can stop you from opening a file. Never open, print,
summarize or paste the people's data files, test sentences, word lists or
sheets — nor an export's `input-words.json`: it lists the words of their
training sentences, and stays beside the model folder, never in it
([serving](/docs/agents/serving#what-an-export-holds)).

**The row check.** As it brings a file in (pairs, a test set or a word list),
`data add` checks its rows against the file's own two columns — no
dictionary, nothing removed. It counts, and names by row number:

- copies: the translation is the source sentence again (a name or a loanword
  is fine; otherwise the translation is missing);
- repeats of an earlier pair;
- translations far longer or shorter than the file's usual ratio (cut off,
  or two sentences in one cell);
- rows that look swapped: the source reads like the file's translations, and
  the other way round;
- runs of rows that look one row off: their translations fit the next or
  previous row better — numbers, question marks and lengths line up one row
  away, and so do the words: how well a row's source words find matches
  among a translation's words, by how often the two occur together in the
  rest of the same file (rarer words weigh more; the row itself left out).
  This finds a shift in a file of templated sentences, whose lengths all look
  alike; it adds nothing when the file's words say too little.

It prints up to 12 row numbers a kind (up to 6 runs for rows one off) — for a
spreadsheet, the row in the person's own file, header counted — and records
the counts in the sidecar's `x-import.quality`. Length, swap and shift checks
need at least 20 pairs; a word list (`--into lexicon`) gets only copies and
repeats. **Note.** Pass the row numbers on: the people look at those rows in
their own file and decide. Never open the file to look yourself.

**ELAN files.** When `data add` cannot tell which tier is which (a side named
by no flag, with not exactly one tier recorded in its language), it refuses
and lists the tiers by number, in the file's order: `tier <n> (<language or
"no language">, <count> annotation(s))`, with `, under tier <m>` for a tier
that refers to another. Pass the numbers as `--source-col` and `--target-col`
(`champollion data add <file> --source-col <number> --target-col <number>`);
the sidecar records the numbers (`x-import.elan_tiers`). A number or id that
names no tier is refused (`no such tier — … Name a tier by its number`), and
so is a tier whose recorded language is not that side's. Two tiers are paired
only when one refers to the other or they share time slots — never by
guesswork. **Note.** A tier's id is whatever the file's maker typed and is
often a person's name, so `data add` never prints it. The person may type an
exact id themselves; you pass the number.
LIFT files are matched by their language codes, Toolbox files by their MDF
markers (`\ge` and `\xe` are English by the standard).

## Transmission modes

Every evaluation resolves its corpus to one mode before anything is sent
(`arena/mt_eval_harness/transmission_policy.py`), and records it in the run
log:

| Mode | When | Remote models |
|---|---|---|
| `cleared` | A licence cleared for redistribution | Allowed |
| `no-train` | A standard Creative Commons non-commercial or no-derivatives licence; or an unregistered corpus that declares no licence | Only over channels that do not train on inputs: OpenRouter pinned to `data_collection: deny`, first-party vendor APIs, or local. A no-training guarantee, not a no-retention one |
| `consent-required` | A modified, bespoke or unstated licence (`LicenseRef-*`) | Refused until the dataset's entry records a `transmission_consent` grant (`granted_by`, `date`, `scope`, `evidence`); local still works |
| `sealed` | A held-out or gold-standard segment, a quarantined set, or a steward's local-only mark | Refused, with no override |

- **Lock.** Text of a `consent-required` or `sealed` corpus is withheld from
  the terminal too.
- An external method (a plugin) on a `no-train` corpus is warned about, not
  refused: the harness cannot see the plugin's channel. On `consent-required`
  and `sealed` corpora it is refused unless `--attest-local-transport`.
- **Lock.** The local provider counts as local only when its endpoint is a
  loopback address (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1`, a unix socket) — never
  because of its name.
- **Note.** Never record a `transmission_consent` grant, and never interpret a
  licence on the rights-holder's behalf. A grant is recorded by the dataset's
  steward once the rights-holder gives it.
- **Note.** `--allow-data-collection` lifts the no-train pin only for an
  unregistered corpus that declares no licence; it asserts the caller holds
  the rights. Pass it only when the person says they hold them.

## Registration tiers

Registering a corpus is optional: the rails never need it. It writes a
metadata card so the corpus can be named, compared and, if its holders choose,
listed. `champollion network register-corpus` is interactive at a terminal
and scriptable with flags (`--tier`, `--data`, `--license`, `--name`, …).
**Note.** The tier, like every term, is the holders' decision.

| Tier | The card | The text | What it refuses |
|---|---|---|---|
| `local-only` (default) | Written beside the `--data` file (or `--out`, or here), never into the shared card folder | Never leaves this computer; the sidecar gets `transmission: local-only` | — |
| `private` | Metadata with `quarantine: true`; from an npm install it stays local, and listing it is a separate request (`champollion network submit --type dataset`) | Never uploaded; no transmission mark — its licence decides the mode | — |
| `public` | Metadata plus a fetch-from-source pointer (`--repo-url`, `--builder`) | Never hosted: fetched from its source | A non-commercial, no-derivatives, restricted or unconfirmed licence (*"Register privately or local-only instead."*); `--data` |
| `sealed` | Metadata with `quarantine: true` and a sealed block (`--seal-input`, `--threshold-pubkey`, `--custodian-group`, `--qualifier-id`) | Only ciphertext exists, written to `<id>.sealed.json` or `--seal-out` | A file that is a byte copy of a public corpus; `--data` |

In every tier nothing is uploaded at registration (`--json` says
`uploadedContent: false`). The one network call, from an npm install, compares
the file's sha256 with the public catalogue's on this computer (the hash never
leaves); with `CHAMPOLLION_OFFLINE=1` the card says the comparison was not
made. With `--data`, the sidecar records `id`, `name`, `license`, `tier`,
`sha256`, `rows`, `card` and `registeredAt`. **Lock.** A registered id is
never re-derived: registering the file again under another id is refused, and
a changed file (another sha256) no longer gets the card's id or grade.

## Outputs are derivatives

A model's output over restricted sentences is a derivative of them, and an
evaluation makes such outputs at scale. The tools treat outputs the way they
treat their inputs:

- For every corpus that is not `cleared`, the run records and prints a notice:
  its predictions are machine derivatives of restricted sentences, not to be
  distributed.
- Where the text is withheld (local-only, sealed, consent-required), every
  file made from it — run logs, reports, comparisons, cache entries,
  `mt-eval translate` output, forge's split sides, cleaned corpora and
  hypotheses — gets a set/1 sidecar carrying the mark (`derived_from`,
  `written_by`). A `no-train` corpus gets the notice but no sidecar.
- A model trained on local-only text writes local-only output (above).
- `mt-eval publish` never uploads a local-only corpus's sentences, even with
  `--publish-entries`, and publishes a coached prompt only as its hash by
  default for such a corpus. For other corpora the prompt is published unless
  `--redact-coaching`.

**Note.** Publishing is the people's decision, made in their words, with the
preview (`--dry-run`) shown to them first. Never publish, paste or send a run's
outputs on their behalf.

===== SECTION: Measurement rules =====

# Measurement rules

The rails promise the people will **know** how good a model is on their own
sentences — not that it is good. That promise rests on a few rules, most of
them enforced. This page states them exactly, and ends with how to say a
number.

## The scoring standard (standard/1)

Every new run is scored the same way (`arena/mt_eval_harness/scoring.py`):

- **The headline:** corpus-level **chrF++** (sacreBLEU chrF with word order
  2), from 0 to 100 — higher means closer to the reference translations —
  with its **95% bootstrap interval** and its sacreBLEU signature. Written
  `chrF++ 47.5 [45.9, 49.0]`.
- **Which segments count:** one rule for the headline, its interval and every
  comparison. A segment whose translation failed counts as an empty output —
  never dropped, never scored as a placeholder; a segment with no reference
  is left out everywhere.
- **The interval:** the headline's own — percentile bootstrap over those
  segments, 1,000 resamples, seed 12345, α 0.05. Below 30 segments the tools
  warn that the interval may have poor coverage; with fewer than 2 there is
  none.
- **Beside it, never blended:** BLEU, spBLEU, TER, and COMET when it was
  computed, each with its signature or model id.
- **Diagnostics, apart:** exact match, equivalent match, FST acceptance,
  morphological accuracy, semantic validator, code-switching, hallucination,
  terminology adherence, writing style. They never enter a headline and never
  rank.
- **"Better" is a paired significance test** on chrF++, never two numbers
  compared by eye.
- **No quality labels.** Only human evaluation certifies quality.

**Retired:** the weighted composite score and the quality-tier labels. A
standard/1 run card carries `composite: null` and `quality_tier: null`.
**Note.** Never present, compute or quote a composite or a tier, even from an
old card.

**Score caveats** are diagnostics written beside a score, never a change to
it: `source_copy` (half or more of the outputs copy the source),
`length_inflation` and `length_deflation` (outputs over twice, or under half,
the reference length — on average, or in a quarter or more of the segments), `near_constant_output` (one output repeated across many
sources), and `train_test_near_twin` (test rows with a twin in training —
major when half or more do). **Note.** Pass every caveat on with the score,
word for word.

## Gated measurement

When a run has a gate chain ([methods and gates](/docs/agents/methods#gate-chains)),
**what is measured is what ships**:

- the headline chrF++ scores the gated output;
- the ungated chrF++, with its interval, sits beside it
  (`overall.gates.ungated`);
- the **refusal rate** — segments the gates refused ÷ segments judged — is a
  number of its own, with counts by gate and by what shipped (`shipped_from`:
  method, source, fallback, nothing);
- the chain's **fingerprint** (sha256 of its canonical JSON) travels with the
  report and any published run.

**Lock.** No fallback in measurement: `mt-eval run` and `mt-eval test` refuse
a chain whose gates hand refused segments to a fallback, before anything is
translated or spent.

**Note.** Report a gated score with its ungated score and refusal rate.
A gated score alone hides what the gates threw away.

## Sets and what each is for

| Role | Used for | Read |
|---|---|---|
| `train` | Learning | Never scored as a result |
| `dev` (practice) | Choosing the checkpoint; judging improve rounds (from 50 sentences); the dictionary floor | Freely |
| `test` | Milestones: testing a model, against the people's prediction | Every scoring read needs a preregistration (forge); every read is logged |
| `sealed` | A test no one outside its holders sees | Once |

**In nmt-forge** (the registry, `.forge/eval-registry.json`; the ledger):

- **Lock.** Every read of a registered set is written to the hash-chained
  ledger with its purpose (`score`, `dev-selection`, `audit`, `inspect`).
- **Lock.** Scoring a test set requires a valid preregistration for its
  current content.
- **Lock.** A sealed set is scored once. A second score is refused (`sealed
  set '<name>' has already been spent`); a single `mt-eval` read of the sealed
  file spends it too. `--override-respend '<reason>'` (on `nmt-forge score`
  and `nmt-forge compare`) is written to the ledger. `export` refuses to
  re-spend and names `--no-eval`.
- **Lock.** The dev fence: training needs a registered `dev` set; dev rows may
  not share an exact source or target with a test or sealed set; no training
  row may be a dev row.

**In mt-eval:**

- **Note.** `mt-eval run` and `mt-eval compare` score a test or sealed file
  without any preregistration and never refuse on read counts. `mt-eval run`
  only appends a line to the file's read log (`<file>.reads.jsonl`) when forge
  created one; `compare` and `test` log nothing. Never score the test set with
  mt-eval before the people's prediction is written.

## Predictions

```bash
nmt-forge prereg new first-model --eval-set project-test --expect "<their words>" --rationale "<their reason>"
nmt-forge prereg new round-2 --eval-set project-test --predictions predictions.json
nmt-forge prereg template --out predictions.json
```

- `--expect` and `--rationale`: one free-text prediction about chrF++, in the
  people's own words. Its verdict is the people's: `nmt-forge prereg verdict
  <id> --prediction <n> --held` (or `--missed`) `--by "<who>"`.
- `--predictions <file>`: a JSON array; each prediction names a `metric` and
  a `rationale`, and either a `direction` (`increase`, `decrease`,
  `no_change`) with a `baseline_score` (and optional `margin`) — judged by the
  tools — or free-text `expect`.
- **Lock.** A prediction written after any scoring read of the set (by forge,
  or by `mt-eval run`) is refused: *"eval set '…' was already read for scoring
  (N time(s): …) before this preregistration"*. `--allow-after-reads` lets it
  through, and every report, export and status says so.
- **Note.** The prediction is the people's, written before any score exists,
  never reworded or narrowed by you. The rails' question suggests no number
  (*"No number is suggested here, so the guess stays theirs"*); do not offer
  one either.

## Near-copies

`nmt-forge leak-audit` compares every training pair with every registered dev,
test and sealed set:

| Found | Rule | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| Same file | sha256 | Dropped |
| Exact copy | Same source or same target after normalization | Dropped |
| Near copy | Target word sets overlap ≥ 0.6 (Jaccard) where one contains the other, or ≥ 0.9 | Dropped |
| Template sibling | Same sentence frame, different answer | **Kept** to learn from, and counted, so the score can be read with and without those test rows |
| Source-only match | Same prompt, different answer | Kept, reported |

Short sentences are compared by character trigrams; very short ones by exact
match only. A test row is a **near-twin** when a training row is identical or
overlaps it ≥ 0.6 on either side; when half or more of the test rows have
twins, the score is mostly recall, not translation, and the caveat is major.
`--clean-to` writes the screened file; `--drop-test-twins` also drops the
training rows that twin a test row, for a twin-free score.

The rails' first dev split applies the same threshold: `--near-dupe 0.6` on
`nmt-forge split` keeps rows whose words overlap ≥ 0.6 on one side of the
dev/training line, so the first dev score holds no near-copy memory a later
round's screen would deny. `--max-group` caps a near-copy group at half the
dev size plus one, so a file written from templates still splits.

**Note.** Say "the leak audit found …" only from `true_now` or the audit's own
output, never "the test set is clean" on your own.

## The dictionary floor

`nmt-forge floor <word lists>` translates the dev set word for word with the
dictionary (longest phrase first) and scores it with the same code as a run's
dev score: chrF++ with its 95% interval. It runs on this computer, never reads
the test set, and records only the dictionaries' names, hashes and entry
counts, how many source words they reached, and the scores. A run **beats the
floor** only when the lower end of its dev interval is above the upper end of
the floor's; `nmt-forge status` warns about a run that does not.

## Comparing two models

**An improve round** (`nmt-forge compare-runs <in-use> <new>`): both models'
translations of the **same dev sentences**, paired row by row; a paired
approximate-randomization test (1,000 trials) and a 95% bootstrap interval on
the difference.

| Verdict | Rule |
|---|---|
| **too-few** | fewer than 50 dev sentences, whatever the scores — the model in use stays, and the speaker's blind marks decide (below) |
| **better** | 50 or more, p < 0.05 **and** the interval's lower end above 0 — the new model is offered for use; it is put to use only on the people's yes |
| **worse** | 50 or more, p < 0.05 and the interval's upper end below 0 |
| **no-change** | anything else — the model in use stays |

**Why 50.** Measured on the invented test language's ByT5-small outputs, 100
random practice sets per size, with this rule: at 23 dev sentences it called
two near-equal models (0.7 chrF++ apart on 500 sentences) different 9 times
in 100, and called a real +5.9 chrF++ gain **better** only 21 times in 100;
at 50 sentences, 4 times and 96 times in 100. The smallest difference seen 8
times in 10 was 8.1 chrF++ points at 23 sentences, 5.8 at 50, 4.0 at 100 and
2.8 at 200. So the rails' first split sets aside at least 50 dev sentences
when there are 200 pairs or more — one in ten of the screened pairs, at most
500; with fewer than 200 pairs, a quarter of them, which is under 50 — and
the review sheets grow the set with practice rows: one row in two while it
is under 50, one in four until it reaches 200.

Each verdict also says the smallest difference its dev set shows reliably
(8 times in 10): the interval's width × (1.96 + 0.84) ÷ (2 × 1.96). When that
is over 3 chrF++ points, "no-change" is the dev set's limit, not proof the
round did nothing. The dev set also chose the new run's checkpoint, which
favours the new model slightly — **say so** when you relay a verdict.

A blind preference by the speaker for the newer model (below) makes forge
offer it for use only after a **too-few** or **no-change** verdict — never
after **worse** — and the people say yes first (`improve-promote`, mode
`confirm`). A blind preference for the model a promotion replaced never puts
it back: the round report's action asks the people.

**Any two runs** (`mt-eval compare <report> <report> --significance`):
approximate randomization by default (`--method paired_bootstrap` for the
other), 1,000 trials (`--n-bootstrap`), α 0.05, seed 12345, on the entries the
reports share by id (a warning under 10). chrF++ first, then the secondary
metrics. Every pair of runs is tested; there is no multiple-testing
correction, and the output says so.

## What the wishlist steers on

`nmt-forge analyze` breaks a run's dev chrF++ down by kind of sentence (with
at least 5 dev sentences of a kind). A kind is **weakest** — and weights the
wishlist — only when the 95% interval on how far its sentences score below
the rest sits wholly above zero (Welch's interval on sentence-level chrF++).
A lower score that could be chance is reported as such (*"… could be chance —
the wishlist does not steer by it"*) and never weights the sheet.

Its "Words it has never seen" section asks for two or three sentences with
each word, each saying something different, not one: on the invented test
language, a word seen once in training came out right 27–29% of the time and
a word seen 2–4 times 63–95%; and at 3,200 training sentences, ByT5-small
trained on sentences chosen for the most new words had 39.4% of 500 held-out
sentences right in meaning, against 53.4% for everyday sentences, at
slightly more of the speaker's time (about 57 hours against 54).

## The speaker's marks

In each improve round the speaker marks the model's drafts of new sentences
`Y`, `N` or `?`. The share right is `Y ÷ (Y + N)` (`?`, unmarked, practice
rows and rows shown again left out), with a 95% Wilson interval. A rise between rounds counts as
**progress** only when the last round's interval sits wholly above the
first's, a round's model was put to use in between — chosen by the people
(forge's `export` and `choose` records), whether after a **better** verdict,
on the speaker's blind marks or by their own choice; a **better** verdict
alone does not count — **and** the speaker's blind checks of each promotion
(below), pooled over the rounds in between, marked the new models right
clearly more often than the ones they replaced (|z| > 1.96).
These are sentences no model had seen: the measure that matters most, and the
one to lead with ([coaching](/docs/agents/coaching)).

**Two models, blind.** `champollion improve sheet` has a second model draft a
seeded random half of the drafted rows (`nmt-forge draft-newer`), unmarked:
the newest trained model when it is not the one in use — as after a round
whose verdict was too-few, no-change or worse — or, on the visit after a
promotion, the model the one in use replaced. Which rows are whose is kept
beside the sheet in `improve/round-<k>/sheet-key.json` (`in_use`, `other`,
`relation` `newer` or `replaced`, each model's training pairs `in_use_pairs`
and `other_pairs`, `other_rows`, and `repeat_rows`, below).
`champollion improve marks` then counts the two models apart, rows shown
again left out of all of it:

- the share right above — the progress measure — counts the model in use's
  rows only;
- every draft marked right and every fix becomes a training pair, whichever
  model drafted it;
- a two-proportion test (pooled, two-sided at 5%: |z| > 1.96) says which
  model the speaker marked right more often, if either: `clear` is `newer`
  or `replaced` (the other model), `in-use` or `neither`, recorded in
  `marks.json` (`blind`) with both counts (`in_use_right`, `in_use_judged`,
  `other_right`, `other_judged`, `in_use_share`, `other_share`), `other`,
  `relation` and both training-pair counts; a comparison with a newer model
  also keeps `newer`, `newer_right`, `newer_judged` and `newer_share`. When
  either model has no row marked `Y` or `N`, `clear` is `null` and the text
  says *"too few rows of one model were judged to compare"*;
- against a newer model, with at least one draft of each judged, the counts
  go to forge (`nmt-forge speaker-verdict`), which runs the same test and
  records `clear` (`newer`, `in-use` or `neither`) in its ledger
  (`improve-speaker`). After a **too-few** or **no-change** verdict on that
  run, `clear: newer` makes forge offer the newer model for use;
  `champollion improve marks` then prints *"forge recorded it: it offers to
  put the newer model to use (the people say yes first)"*
  ([training](/docs/agents/training#the-improve-rounds)).

The rows were assigned at random, on one sheet, judged by the same speaker, on
the family's own new sentences — so a clear difference says something the dev
set may be too small to show, and a change in how kindly the speaker marks
touches both models alike. **Note.** Never tell the speaker which rows came
from which model before their marks are read.

**Rows shown again.** From round 2, `champollion improve sheet` puts back one
row for every 10 new sentences on the sheet (`REPEAT_EVERY`; rounded down,
and fewer when fewer qualify): a draft the speaker marked `Y` or `N` on an
earlier sheet, with its earlier draft, unmarked, at a seeded random place —
never a practice row, a row that was itself a repeat, one already shown
again, or a sentence on this sheet. The sheet's first line, above the
header, says: *"A few rows below come back from earlier sheets on purpose.
Please mark them fresh, as if new: how often the marks agree tells how far
they can be trusted."* It never says which; `sheet-key.json` keeps them as
`repeat_rows` (`row`, `from_round`, `from_row`, and `mark`, the earlier
mark). They cost the speaker about 10 seconds a row.

`improve marks` judges each against the speaker's own earlier mark only: a
repeat is never counted in the round's share, never a training pair again,
never in the blind comparison. `marks.json` gains `repeats`: `shown`,
`judged` (marked `Y` or `N` this time; `?` or blank is shown, not judged),
`agreed`, `agreement` (agreed ÷ judged), `wrong_to_right`,
`right_to_wrong`, `wrong_before` (judged rows once marked `N`) and
`rounds_apart_wrong_before`. It prints *"Rows shown again: the speaker
marked A of J the way they did before (P%) — W once wrong now right, R once
right now wrong. Not counted in this round's share, and not trained on
again."*

Pooled over the rounds, once 10 or more are judged (`MIN_REPEATS`), the
round report reads two things from them:

- **Random error** `e`, from the flips that go both ways alike. Two marks of
  one draft disagree by chance 2e(1 − e) of the time, half each way; with
  d = 2 × min(`wrong_to_right`, `right_to_wrong`) ÷ `judged`,
  e = (1 − √(1 − 2d)) ÷ 2. Error pulls every share toward 50%: a draft truly
  right a share p of the time is marked right e + p(1 − 2e) of the time, so
  at e = 10% "truly 80% right" reads about 74%.
- **Drift**: flips one way beyond the even ones. The report warns that the
  marking may be growing kinder when once-wrong-now-right flips clearly
  outnumber the other way: 6 flips or more and a sign test,
  (`wrong_to_right` − flips ÷ 2) ÷ √(flips ÷ 4) > 1.96.

Its check line: *"The speaker marked A of J rows shown again the way they did
before (P%): about E% of marks go the other way at random, which pulls every
share marked right toward 50% — the projection allows for it."* — and on
drift, *"And W drafts once marked wrong are now marked right, against R the
other way: the marking may be growing kinder, which a rise in the share would
not show."* Under 10 judged: *"N rows shown again judged so far — the
speaker's own marking error is estimated from 10."*

**Where the rounds point.** The round report's projection is made only from
real progress (above) while the share right is under 80%. Learning curves
rise by roughly even steps in log-odds per doubling of the training data, so
it reads the step from the same blind checks after promotions: the sum of
`logit(in_use_share) − logit(other_share)` over the sum of
`log2(in_use_pairs ÷ other_pairs)` (shares clamped to 1–99%), with a 95%
range from each share's variance, about 1 ÷ (n·p·(1 − p)) for n drafts
judged. From the model in use's training pairs it says how many more reach
80% marked right — the estimate — and the speaker's hours at 70 seconds a
sentence. The range covers the step's interval (no upper end beyond six more
doublings) and, once 10 rows shown again are judged, where "truly right on
80%" may sit on this speaker's marks: e + 0.8(1 − 2e) + 0.2 × K, at most
97%, where K is the drift per round (flips beyond the even ones, over how
many rounds apart the once-wrong rows' two marks were) times the rounds
between the first and last marks, capped at ±30%. The fewest is the smaller of the two aims at the step's
upper bound, the most the larger at its lower bound; a fewest of 0 reads
"none". The text then adds *"The speaker's own marking: they marked A of J
rows shown again the way they did before (P%), so about E% of marks go the
other way at random … drafts truly right on 80% may be marked right about T%
of the time on their marks — the range takes that in."* (with, when K is
1% or more either way, how much more or less often drafts once marked wrong
are now marked right); before then, *"(The speaker's own marking error is not yet
allowed for: too few rows shown again have been judged.)"* `report.json`
carries the numbers as `projection_numbers` (`more_sentences`, `range`,
`speaker_hours`).

In simulation — a noisy speaker, the rails' own dev split and these verdict
rules, 200 trials per scenario on two sets of seeds — the estimate landed
within a factor of 2 of the true count 69–78% of the time at 400 new
sentences a round and 53–56% at 800, and the true count fell inside the
range 89–94% and 76–80% of the time (without repeats, 91–93% and 51–54%).
Moving the estimate itself to the speaker's marks helped at 800 a round and
hurt at 400 (within a factor of 2: 64% and 19%), so it stays at the plain
80%. A note that the model "may already be working" was tried and dropped:
it was wrong 2–3 times for each time it was right. A rough guess, said so.

## What the numbers do not say

- A score is for the system on that set, not for any one sentence: there is no
  per-sentence confidence.
- chrF++ measures overlap with a reference. A good translation worded
  differently can score low; a fluent wrong one can score fairly high.
- FST acceptance says words exist, not that a sentence means the right thing.
- Published leaderboard rows are self-reported by default; the verifier
  re-scores submitted outputs against the hash-pinned corpus (within 1.0
  chrF++), and does not re-run methods.

## How to report a number

Every number carries **its unit, what it measures, and the set it was
measured on** — with the set's size and the range when there is one.

| Say | Never |
|---|---|
| "chrF++ 24.1 out of 100 on the 50 practice (dev) sentences, range 20.6–27.6" | "24.1" · "24% accurate" |
| "the speaker marked 9 of 24 new drafts right — 38% (21%–57%)" | "38% accuracy" |
| "no measurable change: on 50 dev sentences only a difference of about 5.8 points shows" | "it improved slightly" |
| "too few practice sentences to tell yet: under 50, no comparison decides — the speaker's blind marks will" | "no change" for a **too-few** verdict |
| "on the 50 locked test sentences, once, against the prediction you wrote: '…'" (their words, read back) | a test score with no set or prediction |
| "blind, on new sentences, the speaker marked the newer model right on 7 of 12 and the model in use on 5 of 12 — no clear difference on 24 sentences" | "the new model is better" from the marks alone |
| "chrF++ 31.0 gated (what ships), 33.5 ungated, 12% refused by the gates" | the gated score alone |

- A range is how sure the tools are, not two results.
- Two scores on different sets are not comparable. Two scores on the same set
  differ only when the paired test says so.
- Quote caveats and warnings word for word.
- Never call a score good or bad; never attach a quality word. A fluent
  speaker decides what is fit to use.

===== SECTION: Training with nmt-forge =====

# Training with nmt-forge

`nmt-forge` trains a model on the people's pairs, inside guardrails: it
refuses what would corrupt a result, and every refusal says what, why and the
fix. It implements no metric of its own — every score comes from the
evaluation engine (`mt-eval`), the same code that scores everything else.

On the rails you rarely type these commands: `champollion next` names them,
and from the `forge` step on it relays forge's own advisor
(`nmt-forge status`). This page is what those steps do.

## Models

`nmt-forge init --model <preset>` writes a preset into `config.json` as
explicit numbers (hashed into every run's identity: a later forge release
never changes an existing project's runs). `nmt-forge use-model <preset>`
switches a project.

| Preset | What it is | Needs | What forge says to expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cpu-tiny` | A small transformer trained from scratch on the pairs, with a 4,000-piece vocabulary learned from the training rows | CPU only · no download | "on ~1–2k pairs: chrF++ roughly 5–30 (the top end only for highly templated data) — memorized phrases and your data's templates, not general translation" |
| `byt5-small` | Google's ByT5-small (300M parameters, reads bytes — no vocabulary to fit), fine-tuned | ~1.2 GB download · Apple silicon or a CUDA GPU recommended | "in forge's own trials it learned far more from the same pairs than cpu-tiny — still measure it against your model in use on your dev set" |
| `byt5-small-lowmem` | The same model, learning rate and length limits, set up for a computer with 8–15 GB of memory: Adafactor, gradient checkpointing, and batches of 4 pairs accumulated 4 times (the same 16 pairs a step) — less memory per step, more time. Not yet measured on an 8 GB computer | as `byt5-small` | as `byt5-small` |
| `cpu-finetune` | A small pretrained Marian/opus-mt model, fine-tuned on CPU. You name the base (`--base`); it is never guessed | CPU only · ~300 MB download | "depends on how related the base's target language is — measure it against cpu-tiny on your dev set" |
| `nllb-600m` | NLLB-200 distilled 600M with LoRA | a CUDA GPU (8 GB+) · ~2.5 GB download | "the strongest of the three when NLLB covers a related language; still measure it — never assume" |

Every preset trains with forge's training extra (`nmt-forge[hf]`), with seed 42.
No preset sets a time budget: that number is the people's.

- **Without `--model`**, `init` writes `cpu-tiny`.
- **`--model auto`** (what the rails pass) reads the memory of the GPU forge
  can train on — on a Mac with Apple silicon, the computer's memory (shared
  with the GPU); with `nvidia-smi` on `PATH`, the largest NVIDIA card's:
  16 GB or more (or memory it cannot read) → `byt5-small`; 8–15 GB →
  `byt5-small-lowmem`; under 8 GB → `cpu-tiny`. With neither GPU, `cpu-tiny`.
  The reason, with the memory it found, is printed (`chosen: …`) and returned
  as `model_choice` in `--json`. It does not test that the GPU works.
  `NMT_FORGE_AUTO_PRESET` overrides it (it must name a preset).
- **The stronger model the rounds offer** goes only to a project whose model
  in use is `cpu-tiny`: `byt5-small-lowmem` where `--model auto` would pick it,
  otherwise `byt5-small` — also on a computer where `auto` would pick
  `cpu-tiny`; the offer's `why` names what it needs.

**Note.** Never describe a preset's expectation as a promise. Measure on the
dev set.

## The guarded loop

Each command takes `--json`; `--workspace <dir>` (default `.forge`) goes
before the subcommand. Forge refuses abbreviated flags.

| Step | Command | What it does | What it refuses |
|---|---|---|---|
| Workshop | `nmt-forge init <code> --dir . --pair <src>-<tgt> --model auto` | Writes `.forge/`, `config.json`, `NEXT_STEPS.md` | An unreadable `--pair`; `cpu-finetune` without `--base` |
| Test set | `nmt-forge registry add project-test <file> --role test` | Pins the file's sha256; starts its read log | Synthetic rows in a test or sealed set; a name already registered with other content (unless `--allow-rotate`) |
| Screen | `nmt-forge leak-audit <corpus> --clean-to <clean.jsonl>` | Screens every pair against every registered dev, test and sealed set; writes a clean copy | Overwriting a file in use (unless `--overwrite`); a result with no training left |
| Predict | `nmt-forge prereg new <id> --eval-set <set> --expect "…" --rationale "…"` | Writes the people's prediction before any score | An existing id; writing after any scoring read of the set, by forge or `mt-eval` (unless `--allow-after-reads`, written to the ledger) |
| Dev set | `nmt-forge split <clean.jsonl> --test 0 --dev <n> --seed 42 --near-dupe 0.6 --max-group <m> --out data/split --register project` | A group-disjoint dev carve, registered as `project-dev`. The rails' `<n>`: one in ten of the screened pairs, at least 50, at most 500 — a quarter of them under 200 pairs ([shell](/docs/agents/shell#build-and-test-a-model)). `--near-dupe 0.6` keeps near-copies (word overlap ≥ 0.6) on one side, the threshold every later round's screen applies; the rails set `--max-group` to half the dev size plus one, so a file written from templates still splits | A side over 1.5× its request, or training keeping under half the rows |
| Floor | `nmt-forge floor <word lists>` | Translates the dev set word for word from the dictionary and scores it the same way as a run's dev score | No dev set registered |
| Check | `nmt-forge preflight run --config config.json` | Runs every gate the run will hit, with fixes; exit 2 if any fails | — |
| Train | `nmt-forge run config.json --detach` | Trains, picks the checkpoint on dev, removes the run's other checkpoints ([disk space](#disk-space)), writes `.forge/runs/<run name>-<8 hex>/` with `run-manifest.json`, `run-report.md`, `dev-outputs.jsonl` | A run that already exists (same config, training files and dev set); a disk without room for it (`disk-room`, before anything is written; `--skip-disk-check` overrides); a run in progress; training rows that leak into a test or sealed set; dev rows in training; data marked do-not-train or quarantined; `terms.training: not-allowed`; synthetic data over its cap; a decode cap too short for the references; unknown config keys |
| Test score | `nmt-forge export <run-manifest.json> --prereg <id> --out export/` | Scores the test set once, against the prediction; packages the model, with `input-words.json` beside its folder — the words it was trained on, so a server can name the ones it never saw ([serving](/docs/agents/serving#what-an-export-holds)) | No preregistration, or several and no `--prereg`; a spent sealed set; a non-empty `--out` without `--force` |
| Choose | `nmt-forge choose <export>/model` | Records the people's choice of model | A folder that is not a recorded export with a model |
| Serve | `nmt-forge serve <export>/model --detach` | Serves it on this computer ([serving](/docs/agents/serving#nmt-forge-serve)) | Off loopback without a token, or a local-only model without `--holders-agreed-by` |

Everything that matters is written to the hash-chained ledger
(`.forge/ledger.jsonl`): registrations, reads with their purpose, predictions,
scores, sealed-set spends, overrides, audit verdicts, the floor, exports,
choices, serves and job starts and exits. The run manifest is the record of a
run.

**Preflight gates:** config (prints the full config hash), workspace match, no
run in progress, dev fence, training data, backend installed, selection
plugins, test near-twins and dev near-twins (warnings), leak audit, training
mix, generation headroom, schedule sanity.

**Decoding.** The final dev decode, the test read (`export`), a model in use
translating the dev set again, and the served model use beam search with
`decode.num_beams` (4 unless `config.json` says otherwise); checkpoint
selection, which ranks many checkpoints, decodes greedily. An export
records `beams_applied`, and `nmt-forge serve` decodes the way the model was
measured: an older export without it is served greedily.

**Length limits.** A model learns from at most `model.max_src` tokens of a
source sentence and `model.max_tgt` of its translation, reads at most
`model.max_src` when it translates, and writes at most
`decode.max_new_tokens` (`byt5-small`: 320 bytes each — about 320 letters of
a Latin script, about 100 of syllabics; `cpu-tiny`: 256 pieces in, 384 out).
Nothing is cut silently: training counts the pairs past either limit before
it cuts them, and the final dev decode counts sentences cut going in and
translations that stopped at the cap. Both go in the run manifest
(`length_limits`), and `status` warns, with the fix: split long sentences, or
raise `model.max_src` and `model.max_tgt` (and `decode.max_new_tokens`) in
`config.json` — training then takes longer.

**Note.** `nmt-forge run` itself does not require a prediction; the rails ask
for it first. Do not train before the predict step is done.

**Note.** `export` is the step that reads the test set. Running it is a
milestone, with the people's prediction already written — never a routine
check.

## Background jobs

`run --detach` and `serve --detach` start a supervised job and return.

```bash
nmt-forge jobs                          # every job: state, stage, step, time left, last sign of life
nmt-forge jobs stop <name> --wait 120   # stop it, and wait up to 120 s (at most 180) for it to exit
```

- States: `running`, `finished`, `refused`, `crashed`, `stalled`,
  `deadline`, `interrupted`, `lost`. `lost` is a job whose supervisor ended
  without a record — including after a reboot, when its process number now
  belongs to another process.
- **One training at a time on this computer.** Training jobs queue
  machine-wide, first come first served (`~/.nmt-forge/machine/train-queue`),
  across every project. A queued job stays `running`, with `queued_behind`
  (the job it waits for) in `nmt-forge jobs --json`; `status` is `training`
  and says whom it waits behind, and it starts by itself. A stop while it
  waits ends it unstarted (`interrupted`); a 24-hour wait ends it
  (`deadline`).
- **Bounds** (training jobs): no sign of life for 15 minutes at startup
  (`--startup-minutes`); no progress for the longer of 10 minutes and 30 times
  the median step time (`--stall-minutes`); a deadline of `--deadline-hours`,
  else the config's time budget × 1.25, else 24 hours. A job past a bound is
  stopped and written down.
- **Stopping**: the run halts at its next step; the supervisor escalates to
  terminate after 60 s and kill 10 s later.
- **The wall-clock gate** (Hugging Face backends): after warm-up, forge times
  the steps, projects the run, and refuses one that will not fit the budget
  (`wall-clock budget exceeded: …`). With no budget set, the limit is a 24-hour
  ceiling.
- While a training job runs, `status` is `training` and the rails step is
  `wait`. A job that failed is a warning on every later status.
- **Resuming.** When the last training job ended `lost`, `crashed`, `stalled`
  or `deadline` after saving a checkpoint, `status` names `nmt-forge preflight
  run --config config.json && nmt-forge run config.json --resume --detach`:
  a new run that starts from the interrupted run's last checkpoint (its
  weights, a fresh optimizer, the epochs it had left), and whose manifest says
  where it resumed from (`resumed_from`). It is never offered after a stop by
  hand.
- Detached jobs are POSIX only (macOS, Linux).

## Disk space

Training writes checkpoints: up to `model.save_total_limit` of them at once
(4 unless `config.json` says otherwise), about 1.4 GB each for ByT5-small.
Before these rules, every improve round of a ByT5-small project kept about
5.6 GB, nothing removed an earlier round's model, and a full disk killed a
run as it saved. Forge's GB is 1024³ bytes.

- **A finished run keeps only its selected checkpoint.** Every other
  `checkpoint-*` folder of the run goes once the checkpoint is chosen:
  nothing reads them again (`export` copies the selected one; the next round
  starts from the model in use). The manifest records `checkpoints_pruned`
  (`removed`, `bytes`, `kept`). `"keep_checkpoints": "all"` in `config.json`'s
  `model` block keeps them all. Any other value is refused when the config
  is read, before any training (`ConfigError`; here for the value `x`):
  `config.model.keep_checkpoints is "selected" (the default: only the checkpoint the run picks stays) or "all", not 'x'`.
- **Lock.** A run the disk cannot hold is refused before anything is written
  (guard `disk-room`); a detached run is refused at once, before its job
  starts. The estimate: one checkpoint's size — the kept checkpoint of an
  earlier run of the same base in this workspace, else the base's own weight
  files (a local folder, or the Hugging Face cache) — times
  `model.save_total_limit`, plus 1 GB to finish; never under 2 GB. The
  refusal reads
  `[disk-room] this computer has <free> free; training this model needs about <need> (<n> checkpoints of about <size> each while it trains, and room to finish)`
  — or, when no size is known, *"(at least that much must stay free
  whatever the model)"* — then
  `why: a disk that fills mid-training loses the run as it saves, and slows the whole computer`,
  and a `fix` that names what `nmt-forge tidy` can free here (when it can
  free anything), moving other files off the disk, and `--skip-disk-check`.
- `nmt-forge run … --skip-disk-check` (with or without `--detach`) starts
  anyway. The manifest's `disk_room` records the check — `free_bytes`,
  `checkpoint_bytes` (`null` when unknown), `checkpoints_at_once`,
  `need_bytes` — or `{"skipped": "--skip-disk-check"}`. **Note.** The
  estimate can be wrong; whether to skip the check is the person's call.
- **`nmt-forge tidy`** lists the model weights of earlier rounds that nothing
  uses — each run with its size, the total, the free space — and removes
  nothing. `nmt-forge tidy --yes` removes them. It never removes the model in
  use, the newest run, or the model the one in use replaced (the blind
  review sheet drafts with it); the output's `Kept:` line names each, with
  why. A tidied run keeps its record — manifest, dev translations, report —
  and its manifest gains `model_removed` (`at`, `by`, `bytes`, `why`); the
  ledger gets a `tidy` entry (`runs`, `bytes`). A tidied run asked to
  translate (`compare-runs` re-translating the dev set with it) is refused:
  `run <name>'s model was removed by nmt-forge tidy on <time> to free disk space — its record stays, its weights do not`.
  **Note.** `--yes` deletes files: show the person the list, and run it only
  on their yes.
- **`status` warns** — a line in `warnings`, relayed by the rails — when the
  disk holding the workspace has under 10 GB free, or tidy could free 5 GB
  or more: *"this computer has X GB free; the models of N earlier round(s)
  nothing uses take Y GB — `nmt-forge tidy` lists them,
  `nmt-forge tidy --yes` frees the space (the model in use, the newest and
  the one it replaced are kept)"* (the part after the semicolon only when
  tidy would free something).

## The improve rounds

Once a model is in use, each round trains a new run on more data with the
same dev set.

**How a round trains.** `champollion improve prepare` runs `nmt-forge
round-plan --config config.json`, which rewrites `config.json` one of two
ways and writes the plan to the ledger (`round-plan`):

- **On from the model in use** (`init_from` its model folder): 4 passes
  (epochs) over all the sentences so far — the old ones keep it from
  forgetting — at half the learning rate. Much shorter than training from the
  start. The full settings wait in `config.json` under `model_full`.
- **From the start**, with the full settings put back, when no model is in
  use yet; when the model was changed (`use-model`, which also drops
  `model_full`); for `cpu-tiny`, whose vocabulary comes from the training
  sentences (it trains in minutes); for an adapter (LoRA) model; and every
  4th round, so many short continuations do not drift.

`prepare` prints the plan and its reason, and records `training` (`mode`,
`epochs`) in `improve/round-<k>/prepared.json`. Either way the new run is
judged against the model in use on the same dev sentences. Then (1, 3 and
4 are states forge's advisor names; 2 is recorded by the rails):

1. **`improve-compare`** (`auto`): `nmt-forge compare-runs <in-use
   run-manifest.json> <new run-manifest.json>` — the two models, paired
   sentence by sentence on the dev set. With fewer than 50 dev sentences the
   verdict is **too-few**, whatever the scores: *"too few dev sentences to
   tell: below 50, a difference is not told from chance reliably, whatever
   its size"*. From 50: **better** only when the paired test's p < 0.05
   **and** the 95% interval of the difference is above zero; **worse** when
   p < 0.05 and it is below zero; otherwise **no-change**. Every verdict says
   the smallest difference its dev set shows reliably. The test set is never
   read. Refused (`improve-loop`) for runs on different dev sets, a run
   without saved dev translations, or a dev set changed since the new run.
2. **The speaker's verdict**, where the dev set could not decide. A round's
   model that was not put to use drafts half of the next review sheet's
   drafted rows, blind (`draft-newer`, below), and `champollion improve
   marks` records the speaker's counts with forge:
   `nmt-forge speaker-verdict --newer <run> --in-use <run> --newer-right <n> --newer-judged <n> --in-use-right <n> --in-use-judged <n> --json`.
   Forge acts on it only after a **too-few** or **no-change** verdict. A
   pooled two-proportion test, two-sided at 5% (|z| > 1.96), gives `clear`:
   `newer`, `in-use` or `neither`; the ledger's `improve-speaker` entry keeps
   the two run names, the four counts, `z` and `clear` — counts only. It
   refuses counts below 0, more right than judged, and a model with no
   judged draft. Its text: *"Marking blind on the same visit, the speaker
   marked the newer model right on A of B new sentences (P%) and the model
   in use on C of D (Q%)"*, then *"the newer model is clearly better on
   these sentences — forge offers to put it to use"*, *"the model in use is
   clearly better on these sentences — it stays"* or *"no clear difference
   on these sentences — the model in use stays"*.
3. **`improve-promote`** (`confirm`), on **better** — or on **too-few** or
   **no-change** when the newest `speaker-verdict` on that run says
   `clear: newer` (never on **worse**). It is an offer: a verdict alone puts
   nothing to use. On the people's yes it exports the new run without reading
   the test set (`--no-eval`), records it as chosen (`choose`), stops the
   running server and serves the new model at the same port. Only that
   `export` and `choose` count as putting a model to use: until then the
   round report reads *"measurably better: not put to use — the people have
   not chosen it"*, and its progress, projection and overfit check leave the
   model out. On the speaker's marks, its `why` adds their counts and *"a
   clear difference: the newer model is better on the sentences the family
   needs"*. On the next sheet, half the drafted rows come from the model it
   replaced, so the speaker checks the promotion blind (below).
4. Otherwise the model in use stays and the next round begins — unless the
   last two round verdicts since the last change of model are both
   **no-change** or **worse**, with `cpu-tiny` in use. The last change of
   model is the newest `model-change` (a preset switch or a `not-now`) or
   `choose` entry in the ledger — any model the people put to use, a
   promotion on the speaker's marks included. A **too-few** round is not a
   judged round: when either of the last two is too-few, there is no offer.
   Then **`improve-stronger-model`** (`ask_user`):
   `nmt-forge use-model <preset> --config config.json --answer yes` (or
   `not-now`), the preset `byt5-small` or `byt5-small-lowmem`
   ([models](#models)). The answer slot is `try_it`. `yes` rewrites the
   config's model (keeping the people's time budget) and the next step trains
   it; `not-now` changes nothing. Both are written to the ledger
   (`model-change`), and the offer returns only after two more such rounds.
   Over MCP, "not now" here is the answer `try_it: "not-now"`;
   `declined: true` is refused on this step
   ([MCP](/docs/agents/mcp#not-now)). Its `why` never says more sentences are
   not helping: when the dev set is too small to see a round's gain, *"small
   gains may be hiding"*; otherwise the rounds brought *"no change the dev
   sentences can see (about X chrF++ points or more): the rounds may be
   adding less than that, or nothing"* — near the top of the curve a round
   adds about half a chrF++ point, under what 200 dev sentences show.
   **Note.** `--answer` defaults to `yes`: always pass the people's answer
   explicitly.

The rails drive the rest of a round (`champollion improve …`): `nmt-forge
wishlist` writes the sheet of what would help most (40 prompts by default, at
least a quarter left open; its words the model has never seen ask for two or
three sentences each, each saying something different — a word seen once in
training is rarely learned
([measurement](/docs/agents/measurement#what-the-wishlist-steers-on))), `nmt-forge analyze` breaks dev chrF++ down by kind
of sentence, and `nmt-forge grow-dev` adds the speaker's practice sentences to
the dev set under the same name — never a row already in dev, never one
whose source is in a test or sealed set. A kind of sentence steers the
wishlist only when it scores clearly below the rest
([measurement](/docs/agents/measurement#what-the-wishlist-steers-on)).
`nmt-forge draft-newer` (run by `champollion improve sheet`) drafts a random
half of the next review sheet's rows with the other model, unmarked, so the
speaker judges both models blind
([measurement](/docs/agents/measurement#the-speakers-marks)): the newest
trained model when it is not the one in use (its round was not put to
use), or, after a promotion, the model the one in use replaced. Its `--json`
says which (`relation`: `newer` or `replaced`, `null` when there is no other
model and every row is the model in use's), with `other`, `in_use`, the
training pairs behind each (`other_pairs`, `in_use_pairs`) and `n`; the
ledger's `draft-newer` entry records the same. How to relay a round:
[coaching](/docs/agents/coaching).

## Synthetic data and back-translation

- `nmt-forge synth <pack> --out <file>` runs a language pack's generator.
  Forge ships no packs. Each row is verified and stamped `synthetic: true`.
- A synthetic file trains as a tagged lane in `config.json`
  (`data.synthetic`, `{"path", "tag": "<synth>"}`). Over 15% of a kind, the run
  is refused unless the config names `mix.synthetic_sample`;
  `nmt-forge sample --cap 0.15 --key kind` draws a capped sample.
- **Back-translation has no command.** It is a library function
  (`nmt_forge.training.backtranslation.backtranslate`): you supply the
  reverse model; it screens the monolingual text against every registered set
  first and tags its output `<bt>`; the output then trains as a synthetic
  lane. No quality filter runs on it. `config.data.monolingual` is refused.
- **Note.** Monolingual text is the people's data like any other: its sidecar
  terms apply, and a reverse model that is a hosted LLM sends it to a provider
  ([data rules](/docs/agents/data-rules)).

## Symptom → cause → fix

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `cpu-tiny` scores between 5 and 30 chrF++ on dev | It is weak by design: a phrasebook for phrases like its training data | More real pairs; on Apple silicon or a GPU, `byt5-small` (`nmt-forge use-model byt5-small`; `byt5-small-lowmem` where the GPU has 8–15 GB) |
| "Good on templates, bad on real text" | Rule R7 (transfer plateau): dev loss bottomed out before the last checkpoint and rose 5% or more. It fires on any such rise, whatever the dev chrF++ did — read it with the dev scores | More real pairs. Shown by `nmt-forge lint <run-manifest.json>`, not by export |
| The score looks too good | Test copies or near-copies in training; or most test rows have a training twin (R4-recall-not-translation, at half or more) | `leak-audit --drop-test-twins` for a twin-free file; report scores with and without the twins |
| A small difference between two models | The interval is wide (R5-low-power, interval wider than 8 points) | `nmt-forge compare` (paired test); for rounds, `compare-runs`. Grow the dev set |
| A round says "too few dev sentences to tell" (`too-few`) | The dev set holds under 50 sentences: no comparison decides there | Nothing to fix: the next sheet mixes both models' drafts blind and the speaker's marks decide; one sheet row in two is a practice row until the dev set holds 50 |
| A round says "no measurable change" | The dev set is too small to see a round's gain | Grow it from the speaker's practice sentences (`grow-dev`, driven by `champollion improve prepare`) |
| Training refused: `[disk-room] this computer has … free` | The disk cannot hold the run's checkpoints | `nmt-forge tidy` lists what earlier rounds' models would free; `nmt-forge tidy --yes` on the person's yes; or free space elsewhere. `--skip-disk-check` only when the person decides the estimate is wrong |
| A run does not beat the dictionary floor | Training learned nothing the word list does not give | More pairs; check the floor's coverage; say so to the people |
| The dev set is saturated | The interval's lower bound is at 99% of the ceiling | A harder dev set; the score cannot rise further |
| Refused before training | See the "Train" row above; `preflight run` names each failing gate and its fix | Follow the fix. A missing training extra: `uv tool install --reinstall --python 3.12 'nmt-forge[hf]'` (or `pip` into forge's own Python) |
| Stopped by the wall clock | The projected run exceeds the budget (24 hours without one) | A smaller model or fewer epochs, or a budget the people set (`model.time_budget_hours`) |
| A background job failed | `nmt-forge jobs` shows `crashed`, `stalled`, `deadline`, `lost` or `refused` | Read its `stderr.log` in `.forge/jobs/<name>/` and fix it; then train again, or resume from its last checkpoint when `status` names `--resume` |
| Training waits and does not start | Another training on this computer is running; this one is queued behind it (`queued_behind`) | Wait: it starts by itself. Do not start another |
| Long sentences come out cut off | The length limits: `status` warns with counts (pairs cut in training, dev sentences cut going in, translations stopped at the cap) | Split long sentences; or raise `model.max_src`, `model.max_tgt` and `decode.max_new_tokens` (longer training) |
| Words come out as unknown pieces (`cpu-tiny`) | The vocabulary is learned from the training rows only | More pairs that use those words; or `byt5-small`, which reads bytes |

## The failure taxonomy

Forge was built from a catalogue of ways a training project fools itself. In
summary — enforced means the tools refuse it:

| Family | Failures | In code |
|---|---|---|
| Leakage | The answer in the training set; near-copies; paraphrases straddling the split; chained templates | Enforced (leak audit, split guard). Template siblings are kept and counted |
| Dev/test contamination | Choosing checkpoints on the test set; spending a sealed set twice; a test score with no prediction; predicting after reading | Enforced (dev fence, eval ledger, preregistration) |
| Tokenizer and orthography | A tokenizer that cannot write the script; mixed spelling conventions | Not checked for tokenizers; mixed conventions are a lint, only when the config names them |
| Synthetic data | Mastering the synthetic mix; early stopping killing a synthetic-heavy run; collapse; back-translation feeding on its own errors | The early-stopping floor is enforced; the rest are lints or tags |
| Coverage | Missing words for the register | A lint, when a plugin reports coverage |
| Measurement | A delta smaller than its interval; one opaque number; metric math outside the engine | Enforced: every score carries its interval and comes from the engine |
| Decoding | Truncated output; checkpoints chosen by loss instead of output | Enforced: decode headroom, generation-metric selection; length cuts counted and warned about |
| Process | Unknown config keys; do-not-train data; runaway runs | Enforced |

Known gaps, with no code yet: tokenizer coverage, back-translation quality,
truncation by register, the gold/synthetic ratio, variance across seeds.

## Output for programs

`--json` puts exactly one JSON document on stdout. A refusal is
`{"error": {"type", "guard", "message", "why", "fix", "how_to_get", "text"}}`
and exit 2 (`details` is added for split and dev-fence refusals). Exit 1 is an
unexpected crash. `nmt-forge run` ends with `RUN EXIT <code>` (0, 1, 2 or
130); `run --detach` returns 0 with the job document. `nmt-forge status
--json` is `{"snapshot", "advice": {"state", "next_command", "why", "ready",
"blockers", "warnings", "answers"}}`.

  — every subcommand and flag.
