===== SECTION: Methods and gates =====

# Methods and gates

A **method** is anything that translates: a trained model, a prompted LLM, a
dictionary lookup, a rule engine, a service, people. A **gate** is a check
between a method's output and what ships. The rails' default method is a
model trained with nmt-forge ([training](/docs/agents/training)); this page is
the format both are written in, and the other recipes.

Every recipe below obeys the [transmission rules](/docs/agents/data-rules):
**a method that calls a model provider sends text to that provider**, and a
local-only, sealed or consent-required file refuses it.

## method/1

`$schema` `https://champollion.dev/schemas/method/1.json`. Required: `id`
(lowercase words joined by hyphens), `name`, `kind` — plus the one setting
that kind needs, checked by the readers with the same messages in both
runtimes.

| `kind` | Required setting | Runs in | Sends text to |
|---|---|---|---|
| `llm` | `model` (an exact id, never an alias); optional `provider` | CLI; harness via `-m` and `--provider` | The provider |
| `llm-coached` | `model`; the coaching goes in `coaching` (`file`, `prompt` or `dir`) | CLI; harness via `-m` and `--coaching-file` | The provider: the sentences and the coaching |
| `mt-api` | `engine` (from `shared/method-registry.json`) | CLI; harness | The engine's service |
| `local-model` | `model` (a Hugging Face id or a local folder) | Harness, in process | Nowhere |
| `nmt-checkpoint` | `model_dir` | Through its service (`nmt-forge serve`) | This computer's server |
| `lexicon` | `dictionary` | Harness, in process | Nowhere |
| `python` | `entry_point` (`module:Class`) | Harness (`mt-eval run --method <folder>`) | Wherever the plugin sends it (`dependency_class`) |
| `service` | `service.endpoint` | CLI (`api` method) | That endpoint |
| `human` | — | People; score their output with `mt-eval test` | — |

Optional: `version`, `description`, `author`, `pairs` (`{source?, target}`),
`decode` (`temperature` 0–2, `batch_size`, `max_tokens`), `card` (what the
leaderboard shows), `dependency_class` (`S` self-contained, `O` open external,
`A1`/`A2` API-dependent, `X` closed), `evidence` (measured runs: `dataset`,
`metric`, `score`, `ci`, `n` — numbers only), `runtimes` (`cli`, `engine`).

**Where a method.json comes from:** `methods/<id>/method.json` in a project;
`nmt-forge export` (kind `nmt-checkpoint`); `mt-eval export --report <report>
--name <name> --type <type> --locales <code>`; `champollion serve
--emit-manifest` (kind `service`). Older shapes (the CLI plugin manifest with
`type`, the harness plugin manifest with `entry_point`) are still read, as
method/0, with a warning. A document that carries `$schema` is read as
method/1 and must validate.

**Which runtime takes which kind.** The CLI refuses `python`, `lexicon`,
`local-model` and `human` (*"runs in the eval engine (mt-eval run --method),
not in the champollion CLI — or serve it and use it through its endpoint"*).
The harness's `--method <folder>` loads only `python`; for any other kind it
says the flags that run it instead.

**Decoding.** The default temperature is **0** (`shared/model-defaults.json`):
one value for what an app translates at and what the harness evaluates at, so
what is measured is what ships — `mt-eval run --temperature` defaults to it.
A pair, a config or a run may set its own.
Model ids are exact slugs, never aliases.

## Gate chains

`$schema` `https://champollion.dev/schemas/gate-chain/1.json`, one file in
`gates/`. Required: `id`, `gates` (one or more). Optional: `description`,
`fallback`.

Each gate: `id`, `kind` (`metric-threshold`, the only kind), `metric` (a
metric plugin's name), `field` (a key in that plugin's per-segment result — a
number, or true/false read as 1/0), `min` and/or `max`, `on_refuse`.

**The rules** (`arena/mt_eval_harness/gates.py`):

- Gates run in order; the **first** gate that refuses a segment decides what
  ships:

  | `on_refuse` | Ships | Counted as |
  |---|---|---|
  | `drop` | nothing | refused |
  | `keep-source` | the source text | refused |
  | `flag` | the output, marked | flagged, not refused |
  | `fallback` | the fallback's translation, if the same gates accept it; refused again, nothing | refused |

- **Lock.** A segment the plugin cannot score is refused (`no_value`, or
  `plugin_error:<type>`) — never shipped as if it passed.
- **Lock.** A gate whose plugin is not loaded, or cannot score here, stops the
  run before anything is translated: *"a gate that cannot judge is never
  treated as passing"*.
- **Lock.** The fallback must run in this process (`lexicon`, `local-model`,
  or a plugin declaring `dependency_class` `S` or `O`), so a refused segment
  leaves nowhere.
- **Lock.** `mt-eval run` and `mt-eval test` refuse a chain with a `fallback`
  gate: *"a fallback is for serving and translating, never for a measurement:
  the score would be partly this method's and partly the fallback's, under one
  name"*. Measure the fallback as a method of its own.
- **Where gates apply:** `mt-eval run --gates`, `mt-eval test <run log>
  --gates` (re-scored without translating again), `mt-eval translate --gates`,
  `mt-eval serve --gates`, and a deployment's `gates`.
- In a measurement, the headline scores what ships; the ungated chrF++ and the
  refusal rate sit beside it, and the chain's fingerprint (sha256 of its
  canonical JSON) travels with the report ([measurement](/docs/agents/measurement#gated-measurement)).
  With `keep-source`, the headline scores the source text where it shipped.
- **Lock.** Every gate needs `min` and/or `max`, gate ids are unique, and a
  `fallback` gate needs the chain's `fallback` — `champollion validate` and
  the harness give the same verdict. Retrying a refused segment with the
  gate's reason is not built.

## Worked example: an FST validity gate

A finite-state analyzer (FST) says whether a word is a well-formed word of the
language. The harness's metric plugin `giellalt_fst_validity` reports, per
segment, `fst_total_words`, `fst_valid_words`, `fst_invalid_words` and
`fst_validity_rate` (0–1). Words are split on whitespace with edge punctuation
stripped; a capitalised word is retried in lower case.

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://champollion.dev/schemas/gate-chain/1.json",
  "id": "fst-every-word",
  "description": "Ship a sentence only when the analyzer accepts every word.",
  "gates": [
    { "id": "fst-all-words", "kind": "metric-threshold",
      "metric": "giellalt_fst_validity", "field": "fst_validity_rate",
      "min": 1.0, "on_refuse": "flag" }
  ]
}
```

```bash
mt-eval setup --status               # the languages with a pinned analyzer
mt-eval setup --fst                  # the analyzer runtime
mt-eval setup --lang <code>          # the language's analyzer, once per machine
mt-eval run --corpus <dev file> --target-lang-code <code> --method local-model -m <model folder> \
  --gates gates/fst-every-word.json
```

- The analyzer is **not bundled**: the harness ships only pins (a file name
  and sha256 per language), and `setup --lang` fetches the analyzer from its
  upstream into `~/.mt-eval/fsts/<code>/`, under the upstream's terms. It is
  run as a separate tool, never linked into the `champollion` CLI.
- A missing analyzer never becomes a zero: as a metric it is marked not
  computed; as a gate it stops the run.
- An empty output scores 0 and is refused below `min`.
- To serve with it, use `on_refuse: "fallback"` and a `fallback` such as
  `{"method": "lexicon", "model": "data/lexicon/words.tsv"}` — for
  `translate` and `serve` only.
- **Note.** FST acceptance says a word exists, not that the sentence means
  the right thing. It is a diagnostic: it never enters the chrF++ headline.

## The recipes

### Coached LLM (`llm-coached`)

A general model prompted with the people's guidance: grammar notes, style,
terms.

```bash
mt-eval run --corpus <dev file> -m <exact model id> --coaching-file coaching.md --glossary terms.json
champollion sync --method llm-coached --coaching-file coaching.md
```

- **In the harness**, the coaching file's text *is* the whole system prompt,
  so it must say what to translate and to output only the translation.
  `--glossary` is a scoring input (terminology adherence), never sent.
- **Lock.** A harness run has one coaching: `--coaching-file`, `--coaching`
  (inline text) or the older `--custom-prompt` — give one. Two together are
  refused: *"--coaching-file and --coaching each give the run its coaching —
  give one (put inline text in the file, or drop the file)"*.
- **In the CLI**, `llm-coached` sends its own prompt with the coaching as a
  "Coaching guidance" block, plus `.champollion/coaching/<locale>.json`
  (`grammar_rules`, `style_notes`, `dictionary`).
- **Note.** These are two different prompts: a coached score measured in the
  harness is not the exact prompt the CLI ships. Say so when you relay one as
  evidence for the other.
- **Sends:** every source sentence and the full coaching to the provider. A
  coaching file with a local-only sidecar runs only on a loopback endpoint
  (`champollion data mark coaching.md --local-only` marks one).

### Few-shot

Examples of good translations inside the coaching. It is a coached LLM: same
commands, same transport — the examples travel in the system prompt to the
provider.

- **Note.** Never take examples from the test set, and never from a
  local-only file for a remote provider. Nothing checks few-shot examples
  against test references automatically.

### Dictionary-augmented LLM

- **CLI:** the `dictionary` in `.champollion/coaching/<locale>.json` is sent
  to every LLM method as "REQUIRED TERMINOLOGY" for the terms found in each
  batch (case-insensitive substring match). DeepL receives it as a glossary.
  Violations are warned about after translating; there is no retry.
- **Harness:** a dictionary reaches the model only as text in the coaching
  file.
- **Dictionary alone:** `mt-eval run --method lexicon -m data/lexicon/words.tsv
  --corpus <dev file>` — longest phrase first, unknown words kept, in
  process. `nmt-forge floor` is this, on the dev set
  ([measurement](/docs/agents/measurement#the-dictionary-floor)).
- **Sends:** the dictionary's matching entries, with the sentences, to the
  provider. A local-only dictionary must not go to a remote one.

### Rule-based hybrid

No rule engine is built in. What exists: `lexicon` (deterministic, in
process); `mt-eval run --method apertium` (a rule-based engine — it sends text
to `apertium.org` unless `APERTIUM_API_URL` points at your own server); and
`python` plugins for your own rules, optionally with an LLM. A plugin class
needs `async def translate(self, entries, config)`; run it with `mt-eval run
--method <folder>`. Validate its output with a gate chain.

- **Sends:** whatever the plugin calls. A plugin is an external method: on a
  consent-required or sealed corpus (local-only included) the harness refuses
  it unless `--attest-local-transport` — which you pass only after verifying
  everything it calls is on this machine.

### Chained methods

Two chains are built in:

1. **A gate chain's fallback:** method → gates → in-process fallback → the
   same gates. For `translate` and `serve` only.
2. **The CLI's pair fallback** (`"fallback": {"method": …}` on an app's pair):
   primary method → the CLI's quality gate → a retry with the gate's feedback
   (LLM methods, or an `api` endpoint that declares `acceptsInstructions`) →
   the fallback once, through the same gate.

Anything longer (generate, edit, validate across models) is a `python`
plugin or a `service`.

- **Sends:** each link sends what its kind sends. A chain is as private as its
  least private link.

### Partial translation (people and machine)

The model drafts; a speaker checks and fixes. On the rails this is the improve
round: `champollion improve sheet` drafts, the speaker marks `Y`/`N`/`?`,
`champollion improve marks` turns fixes and confirmed drafts into training
pairs and practice rows into dev sentences ([coaching](/docs/agents/coaching)).
To score people's own translations as a method (`kind` `human`), run
`mt-eval test` on their outputs. A gate with `on_refuse: "flag"` marks output
for review.

- **Note.** A sentence used to coach or train a method must never be one it is
  scored on.
- **Sends:** nothing beyond the drafting model's own rules; the sheets stay in
  the project folder.

### Fine-tuned model

- **On the rails:** `nmt-forge` (`nmt-checkpoint`; presets `cpu-tiny`,
  `byt5-small`, `byt5-small-lowmem`, `cpu-finetune`, `nllb-600m`), exported,
  served and connected —
  [training](/docs/agents/training), [serving](/docs/agents/serving).
- **An open model you already have:** `mt-eval run --method local-model -m
  <Hugging Face id or folder>` — in process; nothing leaves the machine.
- **An LLM you serve yourself** (Ollama, vLLM, anything OpenAI-compatible):
  `mt-eval run --provider local --base-url http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 -m
  <model name>`. It counts as local only when the endpoint is a loopback
  address.
- **Sends:** nothing off the machine, when the endpoint is truly local.

===== SECTION: Serving and deployment =====

# Serving and deployment

**A deployment is the measurement pipeline on source-only input.** One
deployment/1 file names the method, its model, its gates and the pair. The
same file is tested on a test set, run over a file and served, so what was
measured is what ships. This page is the agent's half of
[Put it to work](/docs/put-it-to-work).

Throughout: a model that learned from sentences marked local-only can repeat
them, so **its output is local-only too**. Every tool below keeps that output
on this computer unless the data's holders agreed otherwise, and
`--holders-agreed-by` records who agreed. **Note.** Pass that flag only with
the name the person gave you, after they said the holders agreed.

## deployment/1

`$schema` `https://champollion.dev/schemas/deployment/1.json`. Required: `id`,
`pair` (`source`, `target`, optional `target_script`), `method` (`method`,
optional `model`). Optional: `gates` (a gate-chain/1 file) and `serve`
(`host`, default `127.0.0.1`; `port`). Paths are relative to the project root,
where the rails run commands. It names no score.

**Who writes it.** `nmt-forge export`, when the export sits inside a rails
project (a `champollion.project.json` above it), writes
`deploy/<name>.json` — `<name>` is `--name` in kebab case, else
`nmt-forge-<run>`:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://champollion.dev/schemas/deployment/1.json",
  "id": "nmt-forge-<run>",
  "description": "nmt-forge <backend> model <run> (<src>→<tgt>), written by nmt-forge export <version>",
  "pair": { "source": "<src>", "target": "<tgt>" },
  "method": { "method": "local-model", "model": "<export>/model" }
}
```

It writes none (and says `no deployment file: …`) when the export is outside
a rails project, when the model was selected under a decode hook (only
`nmt-forge serve` runs forge's hooks), when the config names no pair, when the
document would not validate, or when `deploy/<name>.json` already deploys
another model (never replaced).

**Who reads it.**

```bash
mt-eval run --deployment deploy/<name>.json --corpus <test set>          # measure exactly what it serves
mt-eval translate --deployment deploy/<name>.json --source-file <input> --out <output>
mt-eval serve --deployment deploy/<name>.json
```

**Locks.** With `--deployment`, `run` and `translate` refuse `--method`,
`-m`/`--model`, `--gates` and `--target-script` (*"--deployment … says the
method, its model, its gates and the target script; drop … (or change the
file)"*); `serve` also refuses `--pair`. An input in another pair is refused
(`deployment <id> translates from <src>; this input is in <x>`). A
deployment whose gate chain falls back can be translated and served, but not
measured: `mt-eval run` refuses a chain that falls back
([methods and gates](/docs/agents/methods#gate-chains)).

## What an export holds

`nmt-forge export <run-manifest.json> --prereg <id> --out <dir>` writes:

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `<dir>/model/` | The folder to deploy: weights and tokenizer, `forge-model.json` (what it was trained on, `trained_on.terms`), `DEPLOY.md` |
| `<dir>/model/champollion-plugin/method.json` | method/1, kind `nmt-checkpoint`, `service.endpoint` `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/translate` (port 8378 unless `--port`), `card.commercial_ready: false`, `evidence` with the test-set chrF++, its interval and n |
| `<dir>/evaluation/` | The test-set evidence. Never copy it with the model |
| `<dir>/input-words.json` | The words of the training sentences' input side, one of each, sorted (`words`, `english`, `sentences`, `from`, and `notes` naming a training file that could not be read as the run read it). Beside `model/`, never in it: they are words from the people's data. Written when the export includes the model and its training files are on this computer; otherwise the export's summary says `input_words.written: false` with `why`. `nmt-forge serve` reads it to name the words the model never saw ([below](#words-the-model-never-saw)) |
| `<dir>/README.md` | What the export is |

## `mt-eval translate`

The pipeline over a file, nothing scored. `--out` takes `.jsonl` (one row per
segment: `id`, `source`, `output`, `error`, and with gates `gates`,
`shipped_from`, `fallback`) or `.tsv` (source, tab, output). Without `--out`
it writes `<run id>.translations.jsonl` in the output folder (`-o`). The
output carries the input's terms — and the model's — in a set/1 sidecar.

**Lock.** When the method's output is local-only (or its gate chain's
fallback's is), a destination outside the project is refused before anything
is translated: *"refusing to write …: what this method writes is local-only
(…), and that is outside … — a place the data's holders did not choose. Only
they can agree to that — ask them; if they do: --holders-agreed-by "<who
agreed>" (recorded in the file's sidecar; it stays marked local-only). Or
write it inside the project"*. With the agreement, the sidecar records
`holders_agreed: {by, date}`; the file stays local-only for every tool.

`--json` prints `translated`, `errors`, `out`, `run_id`, `marked`,
`holders_agreed` and `output_gates`. Exit 1 when every row failed. `--publish`
is refused: there is no score.

## `mt-eval serve`

| | |
|---|---|
| Default address | `127.0.0.1:8379` (`--host`, `--port`, or the deployment's `serve` block) |
| What it serves | Only a method that runs in this process: `lexicon`, `local-model`, or a plugin whose method.json declares `dependency_class` `S` or `O`. An LLM or a hosted engine is refused |
| Token | `MT_EVAL_SERVE_TOKEN`, from the environment only. Required to listen on any address other than `127.0.0.1`, `::1` or `localhost`; when set, required on every `POST` (loopback too). `GET /health` never needs it |
| Limits | 1,000,000-byte body, 500 keys, 20,000 characters a string — over any is `413` |
| Gates | `--gates <chain>` (or the deployment's `gates`). Every gate's plugin must judge without references, or it does not start. A fallback is allowed here, and must run in this process |

**Lock — off loopback.** Without a token: *"refusing to listen on … without a
token — anyone who can reach the port could use the method"*. With local-only
output and no agreement: *"refusing to serve on …: what this method writes is
local-only (…), and an address other machines can reach sends it off this
one. Only the data's holders can agree to that — ask them; if they do:
--holders-agreed-by "<who agreed>" (reported on /health), or keep --host
127.0.0.1"*. Output is local-only when a dictionary's sidecar says so (or
cannot be read), or a model folder's `forge-model.json` records local-only
training terms or records none; it is reported as not known (`null`) for a
plugin or a model folder without `forge-model.json`.

`/health` answers `status`, `method`, `model`, `pair`, `deployment` (`id`,
`sha256`), `runs` (in this process — nothing is sent anywhere), `scored`
(nothing), `output_gates` and `gates` (chain id, fingerprint, gates, fallback),
`output_local_only`, `output_local_only_why`, `holders_agreed_by`, `license`
(`AGPL-3.0-or-later`), `source` (the repository) and `version`.

With gates, a refused segment comes back as its gate says: `drop` — the key
under `errors`; `keep-source` — the source; `flag` — the output, the key
named in `meta.gates.flagged`; `fallback` — the fallback's translation if the
gates accept it. Without gates it checks nothing it returns.

## `nmt-forge serve`

```bash
nmt-forge serve <export>/model --detach        # a supervised background job
nmt-forge serve <export>/model --choose        # also record it as the people's choice
nmt-forge jobs                                 # list jobs
nmt-forge jobs stop <name> --wait 120
```

| | |
|---|---|
| Default address | `127.0.0.1`, port `NMT_FORGE_SERVE_PORT` or 8378 |
| Token | `--token` or `NMT_FORGE_SERVE_TOKEN`; required off loopback. `--detach` takes it from the environment only |
| Routes | `GET /` — a try page for the person (no token; it asks for one when one is set); `GET /health`; `POST /translate` (service-api/1); `POST /v1/chat/completions` (OpenAI-compatible); `GET /v1/models` |
| `--detach` | Returns once `/health` answers; stopped if it does not within 120 s. Refused when the port already answers |
| `--no-hook` | Serve without the run's decode hook (said on `/health` and in `meta`) |
| `--allow-locale` | Also accept these locale codes (repeatable) |
| `--device` | `auto` (default) or `cpu`. With `auto`, a server started while a training job of the same project runs takes the CPU rather than share the GPU, and `/health` says so (`device_note`) |
| Limits | 1,000,000-byte body, 500 keys, 20,000 characters a string, 5,000 pieces of model work a request — over any is `413`. The model is asked 32 pieces at a time, so a sentence from another request waits for one chunk, never for a whole request. A request still running after 600 s is refused whole — `503`, *"send fewer pieces at a time"* — never answered in part |
| Decoding | Beam search with the export's `num_beams` when the export records `beams_applied` (as the model was measured); greedy for an older export. Text sent is normalized to NFC, as training data is |

**Lock.** Off loopback, a model whose output is local-only — trained on
local-only sentences, or with no record of what it learned from — is refused
without `--holders-agreed-by`. `/health` reports `pair`, `accepts`,
`decode_hook`, `run`, the dev and test reports, `score_caveats`, `caveats`,
`trained_on`, `output_local_only`, `holders_agreed_by`, `device_note`,
`limits` (`pieces_per_request`, `pieces_per_turn`, `request_seconds`),
`unseen_words_check`, `text_pipeline` and `output_gates`. Every `/translate` answer from a
local-only model carries `meta.output_local_only: true`, and every
`/v1/chat/completions` reply carries `meta.output_local_only` (true or false).
When the length limits cut anything in a request, its `meta.cut` counts the
sentences cut going in (`inputs`) and the translations that stopped at the
cap (`outputs`) ([training](/docs/agents/training#the-guarded-loop)).

**Note.** The try page is for the person. `try_translation` (MCP) sends them
there for a local-only model; never call `/translate` yourself to read its
output ([contract](/docs/agents/contract) §1).

### Words the model never saw

A sentence holding a word the model never saw in training is very likely
mistranslated, however fluent it reads. On the invented test language, a
held-out sentence with a content word the model had not seen was translated
right 0 times in 358 (ByT5-small at 1,600, 6,400 and 25,600 training pairs),
and came out confidently wrong — fluent, every word a real form, the meaning
wrong — 32%, 55% and 83% of the time: the better the model, the more
convincing the guess. So the server names those words.

- **`/health`** says whether it can: `unseen_words_check` is `{on: true,
  words_seen: <count of words in input-words.json>, notes}` or `{on: false,
  why}`.
- **`/translate`** adds, only when a request holds such words,
  `meta.unseen_words` (key → the words of that key's text the model never
  saw, once each, in order) and `meta.unseen_note`. **`/v1/chat/completions`**
  adds the same, keyed by what was asked: `SEG_<id>` per segment in block
  mode, `page` for a page, the JSON object's own keys, or `text`.
- **No record, said on every reply.** The server reads `input-words.json`
  from the folder above the model folder it serves. With none there — an
  export made before 2026-10-13, one made without its training files on this
  computer, or a model folder copied away from its export — every reply's
  `meta.unseen_check` says it cannot check, and why. Serve the model from its
  export, or export it again.
- **The try page** marks the line: *"Never seen in training: … — this line is
  very likely wrong, however fluent it reads."*

A word is a run of letters in any script (apostrophes inside it kept),
lowercased, in NFC. When the input side is English, a plain English ending
counts as seen either way round (`walk` seen → `walked` counts; `walked`
seen → `walk` counts).

## service-api/1 — the `/translate` contract

`$schema` `https://champollion.dev/schemas/service-api/1.json`, held to
`shared/test-fixtures/framework/service-api-vectors.json` (run against
`mt-eval serve` and `nmt-forge serve`).

- **Request** `POST /translate`: `keys` (key → source string; required),
  optional `source_locale`, `target_locale`, `method`, `text_format`
  (`"markdown"` for document text), `instructions` (key → note; sent only to a
  server declared to follow them, `accepts_instructions`). A field a server
  does not use is ignored, never refused.
- **Response:** `200` `{translations, meta}` — `meta` is required; `207` adds
  `errors` (key → `{message}`). Errors are `{error: {message}}`: `400` a
  request it cannot take, `401` a missing or wrong token, `404` an unknown
  route, `413` too large, `500` the method failed — never a partial answer.
  (`nmt-forge serve` also answers `503` for a request past its 600 s limit.)
- **`meta`:** `method`, `model`, `output_gates`, `output_local_only`
  (true, false or null), `cost_usd`; servers may add fields.
- **`GET /health`** requires `status` (`ok`), `pair`, `output_gates` and
  `output_local_only`; optional `output_local_only_why`, `holders_agreed_by`,
  `model`, `method`.
- **The rule:** a server whose `/health` says `output_local_only: true` puts
  `output_local_only: true` in every response's `meta`, and a client writes
  such output only where the data's holders agreed.

## `champollion connect`

```bash
champollion connect <export>/model --app <app folder>
champollion connect <export>/model --app <app folder> --holders-agreed-by "<who agreed>"
```

It finds the `method.json` (the file named, or `method.json`,
`champollion-plugin/method.json`, `model/champollion-plugin/method.json` in
the folder), installs it into the app's `.champollion/methods/`, and points
each of its pairs (`<inputLocale>:<target>`) at it as `methodPlugin`, keeping
the rest of the pair. The app folder needs `champollion.config.json`, and the
method must translate from the app's `inputLocale`.

**Lock.** A model whose output is local-only — known from its
`forge-model.json` (a missing one counts), or from its service's `/health` —
is refused without `--holders-agreed-by`: what it writes into the app's
locale files is published with the app. With it, each pair records
`holdersAgreed: {by, date, method, what}`. It warns, without failing, when
nothing answers at the endpoint (`nmt-forge serve <dir> --detach` starts it)
or when `/health` does not follow service-api/1. `--json` prints `method`,
`kind`, `pairs`, `endpoint`, `answering`, `health_problems`,
`holders_agreed_by`.

## `champollion sync`, driven by an agent

`sync` translates an app's or site's locale files with the methods its
`champollion.config.json` names. It asks nothing interactively.

```bash
champollion sync --dry-run --json      # what would be sent, and its estimated cost
champollion sync --max-cost 2 --json   # stop before any call if the estimate is over $2, or unknown
champollion verify                     # placeholders, scripts, key parity
```

**`--json` output** is one JSON object per line. On stdout: `{level: "info" |
"ok", message}`, events `{level: "event", event: "cost" | "file" | "verify" |
"request", …}`, and last `{level: "summary", command: "sync", …}` with
`dryRun`, `totalProcessed`, `totalFailed`, `totalHeld`, `tmHits`,
`sentToModel`, `verify` (`ran`, `errors`, `warnings`), `failedPairs`,
`locales`, `costEstimate` and more; a dry run adds `preflight`, `realRun`
(`exitCode`, `wouldStop`, `reasons`) and `maxCost`. On stderr: `{level: "warn"
| "error", message}`. A hard error prints a summary with `ok: false` and
`error`.

| Exit | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Clean |
| 1 | A `--redo` or `--force-keys` name matched no key; failures with nothing processed; an error |
| 2 | `--max-cost` stopped it before any call (or the estimate was unknown); or partial: something failed, keys were held back, plural forms are missing, or verify found errors |

A dry run sends and writes nothing, does not verify, and exits 0 unless a
named key matched nothing or there was an error. Verify runs after a real sync
unless `--no-verify`.

**Lock — local-only answers.** For an `api` method, a batch whose
`meta.output_local_only` is `true` is not written unless the pair's
`holdersAgreed` names that method; `sync` says so once, and names the
`champollion connect … --holders-agreed-by` call. Those keys stay
untranslated (or go to the pair's fallback).

**Lock — the `local` method.** The `local` method (an OpenAI-compatible
endpoint) asks the server's `/health` once. When it says
`output_local_only: true` — as `nmt-forge serve` does for a model trained on
local-only sentences — nothing from that server is written unless the pair's
`holdersAgreed` names `local`: *"the model at … says what it writes is
local-only … nothing from it was written"*, followed by the
`champollion connect <the model> --holders-agreed-by "<who agreed>"` call. A
server whose `/health` does not answer or does not say `true` (an Ollama or
LM Studio server, say) is used as before.

**Note.** Connect a forge model with `champollion connect` (the `api`
route): it reads the model's own record of what it learned from, and records
the holders' agreement on the pair under the method it installs.

**Words the model never saw.** When a forge server names keys in
`meta.unseen_words`, the `local` and `api` methods warn with the keys —
never the text or the words: *"<API batch N | Local method>: <n> key(s) hold
words the model never saw in training — very likely mistranslated, however
fluent; have a speaker check them: <up to 20 keys>"* (then *"and <n> more"*).
The translations are still written; the warning is how the people know which
to check ([coaching](/docs/agents/coaching)).

**Note.** Pass on every `warn` line. Machine-translated strings are drafts
until a speaker reviews them; never call them correct.

## `champollion serve`

A different server: it serves an **app project's** own configured
translation stack (method, coaching, translation memory, quality gate) to
other projects. Defaults `127.0.0.1`, port 1822. It requires a bearer token
even on loopback (`--token` or `CHAMPOLLION_SERVE_TOKEN`, at least 12
characters) unless `--no-auth`, which is accepted only on a loopback bind.
`--emit-manifest` writes a method/1 manifest of kind `service` for consumers.
Its `/health` is `{ok, service, version}`, not the service-api/1 health
document, so `champollion connect` reports health problems for it.

===== SECTION: Hosting and joining =====

# Hosting a sealed test, and joining a project

Two lanes beside the build rails. Both are plain `mt-eval` commands; neither
is a step `champollion next` names.

## Hosting a sealed test

**Honest status.**

- It works: preparing a sealed set, a key ceremony, running entries on an
  air-gapped node, verdicts and ranking are all commands with tests.
- **It is not on the rails yet.** `champollion new --kind task` is refused;
  the only journey is the language one. Expect a longer manual walk, and
  follow the [contest runbook](/docs/network/sovereignty/run-a-sovereign-contest).
- **The key shares are held by custodians the organizer names.** Nothing in
  the code appoints or vets them. No community key custodians have been
  appointed for any test.
- **Champollion holds no key share and no private key.** The ceremony runs on
  the organizer's machine, and registration sends only identifiers, digests
  and the qualifier threshold — never a key, a share or the sentences.

**Note.** Hosting decides what happens to people's sentences and who can
unlock them. Every step below is the organizer's decision; run each only
when they ask for it.

### What gets made

`mt-eval contest prepare` splits the organizer's corpus:

| Flag | Set | Who sees it |
|---|---|---|
| `--dev-size` (required) | The qualifier: source and references | Public, released from `<out>/public/` |
| `--secret-size` | The sealed test the contest is registered against | Nobody: sealed in `<out>/local/` |
| `--sealed-holdout-size` (needs `--secret-size`) | A second sealed split, scored but withheld until close | Nobody |

`--seed`, `--qualifier-threshold` (above 0) and `--license` are required — no
licence is assumed. `--custodian-group` and `--threshold-pubkey` are required
(the key the sealed sets are encrypted to). The plaintext of each sealed set
is deleted after sealing; `<out>/local/manifest.json` holds the recipe and
never leaves the machine. Sealing runs `champollion network seal-corpus seal`, so the
`champollion` CLI must be installed.

### Custody

**Threshold custody (M-of-N).** On the air-gapped node:

```bash
mt-eval node ceremony init --dir <ceremony> --set <sealed set id> --group <group id> --quorum 3 --shares 5 \
  --custodian <name 1> --custodian <name 2> --custodian <name 3> --custodian <name 4> --custodian <name 5>
mt-eval node ceremony share --dir <ceremony> --custodian <name 1> --dest <their token>
mt-eval node ceremony verify --dir <ceremony> --share <a> --share <b> --share <c>
mt-eval node ceremony share --dir <ceremony> --wipe-originals
```

`init` generates the key, splits it with Shamir's scheme and zeroes it in one
call; it writes `ceremony.json` (the public record) and one share file per
custodian. `--set` must be the secret set's id and `--group` the
`--custodian-group` prepare will use — prepare does not check them, and a
mismatch is found only when a run is refused. Give prepare the ceremony's
record: `--threshold-pubkey <ceremony>/ceremony.json`.

**Lock.** A sealed set is decrypted only by `mt-eval node run-method <id>
--offline --share … --share …` with at least M shares from distinct
custodians whose ids match the set. Threshold custody runs only on this
offline lane.

**Single key.** `champollion network seal-corpus keygen --out <dir>` makes one
keypair; whoever holds its key file can decrypt alone. It is what the
connected node lane uses.

### The organizer's walk (threshold custody)

```bash
mt-eval node bundle --out <bundle>                    # on a connected machine: the node's install
mt-eval node bundle --verify <bundle>                 # on the node
mt-eval node keygen --out <keys>
# the ceremony, above
mt-eval contest prepare --corpus master.json --slug <slug> --name "<name>" --pair '<src>><tgt>' \
  --dev-size <n> --secret-size <n> --seed <n> --qualifier-threshold <chrF++> --license <licence> \
  --custodian-group <group id> --threshold-pubkey <ceremony>/ceremony.json --out ./<slug> --no-register
mt-eval contest register --manifest ./<slug>/local/manifest.json
mt-eval node init --from-contest ./<slug>
mt-eval node egress-check
mt-eval node import-bundle <exchange>                 # entries, carried in
mt-eval node run-method <request id> --offline --share <s1> --share <s2> --share <s3>
mt-eval node export-scores <exchange>
mt-eval node verdicts --contest <slug> --out verdicts.json --metric chrf_plus_plus --tie-test ar \
  --alpha <a> --n-resamples <n> --seed <n>
mt-eval contest rank <slug>
mt-eval contest close <slug> --node-verdicts verdicts.json --verify-key <score-signing public key>
```

`node init --from-contest` sets threshold custody when the set was sealed to
a ceremony key. Entrants qualify on the public dev set (`mt-eval contest
qualify`) and submit methods or models (`mt-eval contest submit-method`,
`mt-eval contest submit-model`, both with an `--offline --bundle-out` path).
The [node guide](/docs/network/sovereignty/sovereign-eval-node) has every
node command.

### What needs a connection, and whose

| Works offline | Needs a sign-in | Needs the database's service key |
|---|---|---|
| `contest prepare --no-register`, `contest qualify` (with `--offline-qualifier-id`, `--offline-threshold`), `contest validate`, `submit-* --offline`, every `node ceremony`, `node seal`, `node keygen`, `node init`, `node import-bundle`, `node run-method --offline`, `node export-scores`, `node verdicts`, `node egress-check` | `contest register`, `contest create`, online `submit-*`, `contest open-intake`, `contest close-intake`, `contest close` | `contest prepare` without `--no-register` or `--self-serve`, `node serve`, `node list`, `node approve`, `node deny`, online `node run-method`, `node relay`, and `contest close` when results were withheld |

The service key belongs to whoever runs the database. An outside organizer
runs these against a database of their own (`MT_EVAL_SUPABASE_URL` and its
keys), or keeps to the offline lane — whose scores are verifiable from their
signed manifests but get no public board entry. **Note.** Never set
`MT_EVAL_ALLOW_PROD`: it lifts the tools' refusal to write to the default
production database, and that is not an agent's call.

## Joining a project

A **registered project** is a language project its owner listed so others
can help, with files: sentences, word lists or methods (review time and
computing are not offered yet). The `mt-eval
project` commands below talk to the project database
(`MT_EVAL_SUPABASE_URL`). Every subcommand except `list` (anonymous) and
`review` (the operator's) signs in (a cached
session, `MT_EVAL_REFRESH_TOKEN`, or an interactive GitHub or Google
sign-in); the account is the sign-in's email.

**The rules.**

- **Reviewed before listing.** A new project starts `pending_review`; it is
  listed only after review. An owner can close a project, never list it.
- **The owner is named as they choose** (`--owner-name`). The project row
  holds no email; the owner's account is kept apart, readable only by them.
- **No email in a listing.** `project list` is anonymous and shows names and
  counts; `project offers` prints helpers by the name they gave (`--as`).
  The owner's account can still read a helper's account email in the offer's
  record, and the consent note records both accounts.
- **Offers are held by both.** Accepting writes a consent note naming who
  submitted it and who authorized it.
- **Nothing is printed from a file.** Names, counts and states only.

### Owner

```bash
mt-eval project register --project . --name "<project name>" --owner-name "<as they want to be named>" \
  --purpose "<what the translations are for>"
mt-eval project ask <slug> --kind sentences --what "<what would help>" --how-many 200 --terms "<their terms>"
mt-eval project offers <slug>
mt-eval project accept <offer id> --into .
mt-eval project decline <offer id> --why "<reason>"
```

- `register` reads the pair from `champollion.project.json` (and the purpose,
  unless `--purpose`); optional `--slug`, `--domain`, `--register`, `--about`.
  At most 5 registrations per account per 24 hours.
- `ask` `--kind` is `sentences`, `word-list` or `method`; asks show only while
  the project is listed.
- `accept` downloads the file, **verifies its sha256** (refused on a
  mismatch), writes `inbox/offer-<offer id>-<file name>` and
  `consent/offer-<offer id>.json` (`offer_id`, `file`, `sha256`,
  `submitted_by`, `authorized_by`, `terms`, `note`, `held_by`), then marks the
  offer accepted. The file then comes in like any other —
  `champollion data add inbox/<file>` — and its holders' terms are asked.
- **Note.** The helper's `--terms` are in the consent note. The answers you
  record with `champollion data mark` must not loosen them.

### Helper

```bash
mt-eval project list
mt-eval project offer <slug> <file> --as "<your name>" --terms "<what it may be used for>" --ask <ask id> --note "<note>"
mt-eval project withdraw <offer id>
```

- `offer` uploads one non-empty file of at most 50 MB to the project's
  private storage, with its sha256, to a listed project only. At most 24
  offers per helper per 24 hours.
- An offer moves once: `offered` → `accepted`, `declined` or `withdrawn`.
- **Note.** Withdrawing or declining changes the offer's state; it does not
  delete the uploaded file from storage. Say so before a helper offers
  anything they may want back.
- **Lock.** `offer` reads the file's sidecar before uploading anything. It
  refuses a `local-only` file, a `sealed` set, and a file whose
  `speakers_agreed` is `not-yet` or `some-said-no`; an unreadable sidecar
  stops the offer. There is no override: the mark is the holders' to change.
  A `training: not-allowed` term is added to the offer's terms, so the owner
  sees it.
- **Note.** An offer sends the file off the helper's computer to the project
  database's storage. Ask the helper, and never offer a file for them.

`mt-eval project review` is the database operator's (it uses the service
key). It is not an agent's command.

  [Join a project](/docs/join-a-project) — the people's versions.

  and [the sovereign eval node](/docs/network/sovereignty/sovereign-eval-node).

  local-only files.

===== SECTION: Coaching the people =====

# Coaching the people

The rails measure. You relay. Most of what the people hear about their
translator comes through you, so the way you say it is part of the work. This
page is how to say it: what the round report holds, how to pass it on, how to
ask for time, and the words to use.

The rules underneath are in [the contract](/docs/agents/contract) §5: say only
what is true, pass on every caveat word for word, promise process and never
quality, give every number its unit and the set it was measured on.

## The round report

Each improve round ends with `champollion improve report` (the journey's
`improve-report` step, mode `auto`). It writes
`improve/round-<k>/report.json` and prints four parts; `--json` prints the
same object:

| Field | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `round` | The round under way: one past the rounds forge has judged |
| `progress` | Lines, in order: the trend in the speaker's marks, then each round's marks (each followed, in a round whose sheet mixed in another model's drafts, by the blind comparison), then each round's verdict on the dev set |
| `checks` | Warnings about what the numbers can and cannot show |
| `projection` | A rough guess at how many more training sentences reach "working", counted per doubling of them, with a range — or why there is none — or `null` before two rounds of marks |
| `projection_numbers` | The same guess as numbers: `more_sentences`, `range` (`[fewest, most]` training sentences; `most` is `null` when the checks cannot bound it) and `speaker_hours` — or `null` when there is no projection |
| `actions` | One to four things to do next |

It reads only records the rounds keep — the speaker's `marks.json` per round
and forge's `improve-compare` verdicts — and prints counts and percentages,
never a sentence.

### What each line means

**The speaker's marks — the measure that matters.** Each round, the model in
use drafts the sentences the family wrote, and the speaker marks each draft
`Y` (right), `N` (wrong, with how it is said) or `?` (unsure). The share right
is counted over the drafts marked `Y` or `N`, with a 95% Wilson interval:

> Round 1: the speaker marked 9 of 24 drafts of new sentences right — 38%
> (95% range 21%–57%).

These are new sentences — drafted before any model learned them — so this is
the out-of-sample measure. In a round whose sheet mixed in another model's
drafts, these counts are the model in use's rows only. Rows shown again
(below) are never in them.

**Rows shown again.** From round 2, about one row in ten is a draft the
speaker already marked on an earlier sheet, back unmarked. The sheet says so
at its top — *"A few rows below come back from earlier sheets on purpose.
Please mark them fresh, as if new: how often the marks agree tells how far
they can be trusted."* — and never says which. `improve marks` prints *"Rows
shown again: the speaker marked A of J the way they did before (P%)"*, with
the flips each way. These rows are never counted in the round's share and
never trained on again; they cost the speaker about 10 seconds a row
([measurement](/docs/agents/measurement#the-speakers-marks)).

**The blind comparison.** A second model drafts a random half of a sheet's
drafts, unmarked, and the speaker judges both without knowing which is which
([measurement](/docs/agents/measurement#the-speakers-marks)). The second
model is the newest one when it was not put to use; on the visit after a
promotion, it is the model the new one replaced. The report adds a line:

> Round 2: Blind, on new sentences: the model in use was marked right on 5
> of 12 (42%), the newer model (not in use) on 7 of 12 (58%) — no clear
> difference on 24 sentences.

After a promotion it reads *"the model put to use last was marked right on …,
the model it replaced on …"*. It ends in one of three ways (a two-proportion
test at 5%): for a newer model, *the newer model is clearly better on the
sentences the family needs* or *the model in use is clearly better*; after a
promotion, *the new model is clearly better on the sentences the family
needs* or *the model it replaced was clearly better — the new one has not
helped on the sentences the family needs*; or *no clear difference on N
sentences*. With too few marked rows of one model it says *"too few rows of
one model were judged to compare"*.

**The trend.** The report calls a rise *real progress* only when all three
hold:

- the last round's range sits wholly above the first round's (its lower end
  above the first's upper end);
- a round's model was put to use in between — chosen by the people
  (forge's `export` and `choose` records): after a **better** verdict and
  their yes, on the speaker's blind marks, or by their own choice. A
  **better** verdict alone does not count; and
- marking blind on the same visits, the speaker marked the new model right
  clearly more often than the one it replaced (the checks after each
  promotion, pooled; a two-proportion test at 5%).

The third is there because a speaker's marking can drift: one who grows
kinder each round lifts every share, but on one visit it touches both models
alike. In a simulation with a speaker who marks 10% of drafts wrongly and
grows kinder each round, a promotion the practice set got wrong by chance
read as real progress in 106 of 1,600 reports where the model could not
improve; with the blind check, 3 — and at most 3 in 1,600 again when rerun
with the 50-sentence floor and the speaker's verdict, including runs whose
practice set starts at 30 sentences.

A rise with a promotion but without that check is printed as *not yet
counted as real progress: how kindly drafts are marked may have changed too*
— with the check's counts, or saying the next sheet mixes the two models'
drafts. A rise with the same model in use is printed as *not counted as
progress*: the sentences or the marking changed, not the model. A rise inside
the ranges is printed as *up, though not yet beyond the uncertainty*.

**The dev-set verdict.** Forge compares the new model with the one in use on
the same dev (practice) sentences, sentence by sentence:

> Round 1: on the same 50 practice (dev) sentences, chrF++ (0–100, overlap
> with the checked translation) 24.1 for the new model against 22.0 for the
> model in use — no measurable change: not used (on 50 sentences only a
> difference of about 5.8 points or more shows reliably).

How the line ends depends on the verdict and on whether the people chose
the round's model (forge's `export` and `choose` records) — a verdict alone
puts nothing to use:

| Verdict | Not chosen | Chosen |
|---|---|---|
| **better** | *measurably better: not put to use — the people have not chosen it* | *measurably better: put to use* |
| **worse** | *measurably worse: not used* | *measurably worse — put to use …* |
| **no-change** | *no measurable change: not used* | *no measurable change — put to use …* |
| **too-few** | *too few practice sentences to tell (under 50): the speaker's blind marks decide* | *too few practice sentences to tell (under 50) — put to use …* |

"Put to use …" ends *on the speaker's blind marks* when forge holds a
speaker verdict for that model with `clear: newer` (`improve-speaker`), and
*by the people's own choice* otherwise. `champollion improve status` uses the
same words: each round's line ends *"· new model on the practice (dev)
sentences: …"*. The verdict rule is in
[measurement](/docs/agents/measurement#comparing-two-models).

**The checks.**

- *Overfitting.* If the dev chrF++ of the model in use rose 3 points or
  more across the rounds (the last round's new model counts only once the
  people chose it) while the speaker's share right rose 2 points or less,
  the report says the gain may belong to the practice sentences, and to
  trust the marks.
- *A dev set too small to see a gain.* When the smallest difference the dev
  set shows reliably is more than 3 chrF++ points (or, unknown, under 50
  sentences), the report says "no measurable change" is the dev set's limit,
  not proof the round did nothing.
- *How far the marks can be trusted.* Once 10 rows shown again are judged,
  over all rounds: *"The speaker marked A of J rows shown again the way they
  did before (P%): about E% of marks go the other way at random, which pulls
  every share marked right toward 50% — the projection allows for it."* When
  once-wrong drafts now marked right clearly outnumber the other way (a sign
  test at 5%, 6 flips or more), it adds *"the marking may be growing kinder,
  which a rise in the share would not show"*. Before 10: *"N rows shown
  again judged so far — the speaker's own marking error is estimated from
  10."*

**The projection.** Made only when the rise is real progress (all three
above) and the share right is still under 80% — the rails' word for
*working* on the sentences the family needs. Learning curves rise by roughly
even steps per doubling of the training sentences, so it reads the step from
the speaker's blind checks of each new model against the one it replaced
(both models' training pairs recorded) and says how many more training
sentences reach 80% marked right, with a range, and the speaker's hours at
about 70 seconds a sentence (a minute to write, ten seconds to mark). The
range covers what the checks allow (95%) and, once 10 rows shown again are
judged, where "truly right on 80%" may sit on this speaker's own marks; the
text then says *"drafts truly right on 80% may be marked right about T% of
the time on their marks — the range takes that in"*. Before then it says
*"(The speaker's own marking error is not yet allowed for: too few rows
shown again have been judged.)"* The estimate itself stays at the plain
80%. Counts are rounded to two figures. When the checks cannot bound it, it
says they *"cannot yet say how many more it could take"*. Otherwise it says
why there is none — for one, *"the speaker's blind check has not yet shown
the new model beating the one it replaced, so the rise may be in the
marking, not the model"*. Always say it is a rough guess; the report does.
In simulation it landed within a factor of 2 of the true count 69–78% of the
time at 400 sentences a round and 53–56% at 800, and the true count fell
inside the range 89–94% and 76–80% of the time (at 800 a round, 51–54%
before the range took in the speaker's marks); the straight line it
replaced, 5% at 400. Never say a model "may already be working" from the
speaker's marking error: the report does not, because in simulation that
note was wrong 2–3 times for each time it was right.

**The actions.** In priority, at most four: mark this round's sheet, or write
the sentences still missing (20 a round); when the blind comparison found the
newer model clearly better, that *"the round did help, even where the
practice set could not show it"* — keep going, and growing the practice set
lets the next verdict see it; when the speaker marked the model a promotion
replaced clearly better, to ask the people whether to put the earlier model
back, and to make the practice set more like the sentences they need; grow
the practice set, when it is too small to see a round's gain and under 200
sentences (*"one sentence in 2 on each sheet has no draft — the speaker
writes how it is said, and it joins the practice set (now 31; 50 lets a
round be judged at all, 200 lets a gain of about 3 points show)"* — "in 4"
from 50); what to do after two rounds without a gain (below); that
the time the speaker said they can give looks too small; and, once the lower
end of the share right reaches 70%, a check on the locked test set — with a
prediction written first.

**Two rounds without a gain** — the last two verdicts both **no-change** or
**worse** (a **too-few** round says nothing either way, and does not count),
with no model put to use between them; forge counts the same way for the
stronger-model offer. Where the practice set can see a round's usual gain,
the action reads *"Two rounds without a gain this practice set can see
(about X chrF++ points or more): the rounds may be adding less than that, or
nothing — it cannot tell which. Faster ways forward: the stronger model the
rails offer when the computer can train one, or more of the kinds of sentence
it gets wrong."* (X is the verdict's smallest difference it shows.) Where it
cannot, it says to keep going. Never say or imply that more sentences will not
help: near the top of the curve a round adds about half a chrF++ point, under
what 200 practice sentences can show. In simulated rounds, the older line
"more of the same may not help" was said in 98 of 1,200 reports while the
model was really improving.

### How to pass it on

1. **Progress first.** Lead with what moved, in the speaker's marks.
2. **Every number with its unit and set.** "9 of the 24 new sentences the
   speaker checked were right — 38%", never "38%". "chrF++ 24.1 out of 100 on
   the 50 practice sentences", never "24.1". A range is how sure the tools are,
   not two results: "somewhere between 21% and 57% — with 24 sentences, the
   tools can't be surer than that".
3. **The checks, plainly.** If the report warns, say what it warns.
4. **The next steps as things they can do.** Turn each action into a sentence
   addressed to the people, with the file it names.
5. **Pass on every caveat word for word.**

**Encourage what is measured.** A draft marked right, a rise beyond the
ranges, a new model put to use: say so warmly. The first translation is worth
celebrating. Never celebrate a number the report does not call progress.

**"No measurable change" — plainly and kindly.** It does not mean the round
was wasted. Say what it means: on this many practice sentences, only a
difference of about this size shows; a smaller gain may be hiding; the model
in use stays in use; the sentences the speaker fixed still count. Then say
the next step.

**"Too few practice sentences to tell" — not "no change".** Under 50
practice sentences no comparison decides, whatever the two scores are; it is
not a verdict about the new model. Say what happens instead: the model in use
stays for now; the next sheet mixes the newer model's drafts in, unmarked,
and the speaker's marks decide; one sheet row in two has no draft, and those
sentences grow the practice set until a round can be judged on it.

**The blind comparison — with both counts, and what it does.** Say
both models' counts and the report's ending, as written. When the newer model
is clearly better, say it as the report does — the round did help, even where
the practice set could not show it — and that it is the speaker's own
judgement on new sentences. After a **too-few** or **no-change** verdict on
that model, a clear preference makes forge offer it for use: `improve marks`
prints *"forge recorded it: it offers to put the newer model to use (the
people say yes first)"*, and the offer comes as the `improve-promote` step
(below) — ask before running it. After a **worse** verdict it is not
offered. After a promotion, the same check is what lets the report count a
rise as real progress; when it says the model it replaced was clearly
better, ask the people whether to put the earlier model back — never do it
without their yes. "No clear difference" on 24 sentences means what it says.
**Note.** Never tell the speaker which rows came from which model before
their marks are read.

**Rows shown again — what they are for.** Say the agreement with its counts,
as the report does ("the speaker marked 17 of 20 rows shown again the way
they did before — 85%"), and what it is for: how far the marks can be
trusted. It is announced on the sheet, not a hidden check of the speaker.
Say the random error the way the report does: about E% of marks go the
other way at random, which pulls every share toward 50%, and the projection
allows for it. When the report says *"the marking may be growing kinder"*,
say it plainly and without blame: a rise in the share may then be the
marking, not the model. **Note.** Never tell the speaker which rows come
back, or what they marked before — the sheet says only that a few rows do.

**Words the model never saw.** When `sync` warns that keys *"hold words the
model never saw in training — very likely mistranslated, however fluent"*,
say it plainly: those lines are very likely wrong even if they read well; a
speaker should check them, or the next round's sentences can teach those
words. Name the keys, as the warning does; you never see the words. The
person sees them on the model's try page, under each line. The evidence, on
the invented test language: sentences holding a word the model had not seen
were right 0 times in 358 ([serving](/docs/agents/serving#words-the-model-never-saw)).

**The wishlist's words.** Its "Words it has never seen" section asks for
*"two or three sentences with each word you need, each saying something
different"*: fewer words, each in a few sentences, teach the model more than
many words once. Relay it that way. On the invented test language, a word
seen once in training came out right 27–29% of the time, and seen 2–4 times
63–95%; and with 3,200 training sentences, ByT5-small trained on sentences
chosen for the most new words had 39.4% of 500 held-out sentences right in
meaning, against 53.4% for everyday sentences — at slightly more of the
speaker's time (about 57 hours against 54).

Never call a score good or bad yourself. A fluent speaker decides what is fit
to use.

## Asking for time

The `improve-time` step (mode `ask_user`) asks how much time the speaker can
give: `per_week` and `total`, each **exactly as they said it** ("maybe 30
sentences a week", "a few hours, then we'll see"). It is recorded by
`champollion improve time` in `improve/time.json`; each round's sentence
count is planned around it, and the report compares the projection with it.

- **Note.** Ask once; never press for more. If they don't know, pass what they
  said — vague words are an answer.
- **Note.** When the report says the projection needs more sentences than the
  time they said is left, tell them plainly, with the options it names: more
  speakers, helpers on the project, or a narrower goal for now (a phrasebook
  for the sentences they need most). Then let them choose.

## The offers the rails make

**Offering a better model for use** (forge state `improve-promote`, mode
`confirm`). A new model was measurably better on the dev set — or the dev
set could not decide (**too-few**, or **no-change**) and the speaker, marking
blind, marked it right clearly more often. Then forge's `why` adds the
speaker's counts: *"Marking blind on the same visit, the speaker marked the
newer model right on A of B new sentences (P%) and the model in use on C of
D (Q%) — a clear difference: the newer model is better on the sentences the
family needs."* Say which it was. It is an offer: a verdict alone changes
nothing. Using it changes what their page or app answers, so ask before
running the step; on "not now", `declined: true`. Only their yes — the step's
`export` and `choose` — puts it to use; until then the report reads
*"measurably better: not put to use — the people have not chosen it"*, and
no rise counts as progress from it. Once chosen on the speaker's marks, the
round's line reads *"put to use on the speaker's blind marks"*.

**A stronger model** (forge state `improve-stronger-model`, mode `ask_user`).
After two rounds in a row that the dev set could judge show no gain —
both **no-change** or **worse**; a **too-few** round does not count —
counted from the last change of model (a switch of preset, or any model the
people put to use with `choose`, a promotion on the speaker's marks
included), with the tiny model in use, the rails offer ByT5-small
— `byt5-small`, or `byt5-small-lowmem` where the GPU has 8–15 GB of memory
to train with (less memory per step, slower): a download of about 1.2 GB and
longer training, best on Apple silicon or an NVIDIA GPU
([training](/docs/agents/training#models)). The answer slot is `try_it`:
`yes` or `not-now`. Say what forge's `why` says — when the dev set is too
small to see a round's gain, that small gains may be hiding; otherwise, that
the two rounds brought *"no change the dev sentences can see (about X chrF++
points or more): the rounds may be adding less than that, or nothing"*. It
does not say more sentences are not helping, and neither do you. "Not now"
is one of this step's answers: pass `try_it: "not-now"` (over MCP,
`declined: true` is refused here). Forge records it, keeps the model in use,
and the offer returns only after two more such rounds (**no-change** or
**worse**). Either answer is fine; it is theirs.

**Judging the prediction.** After a test-set score, the people say whether
the prediction they wrote held (`held` or `missed`) and who judged it. Read
them the prediction and the score with its range; never judge it for them.

**Speakers who have not agreed yet.** A file in `waiting_for_agreement` is
asked about once a session, gently. Only a yes from the person — that
everyone whose words are in it agreed — answers it.

## Words for the people

| Say | Instead of |
|---|---|
| "a score out of 100 for how close the translations come to the speaker's own — chrF++" | "chrF++ 24.1" alone |
| "how sure the tools are: somewhere between 21% and 57%" | "CI [0.21, 0.57]" |
| "the practice sentences" (the dev set) | "dev split" |
| "the test sentences, kept locked" | "held-out test set" |
| "the first small model" | its folder or run name |
| "no measurable change — on 50 practice sentences, only a difference of about 6 points shows" | "no improvement" |
| "too few practice sentences to tell yet — under 50, the speaker's own marks decide" | "no change" for a too-few verdict |
| "a phrasebook: good with sentences like the ones it learned" | "low-resource NMT baseline" |
| "the speaker marked 9 of 24 right" | "accuracy 38%" |

Explain a term the first time it appears, with an example before the word.

## When to suggest help

- **The project is stuck, or they ask for help from people.** Say: *"Having
  trouble, or want help with your project? Let's talk."* —
  [info@champollion.dev](mailto:info@champollion.dev). Never required; no
  pricing.
- **They need more sentences, speakers or computing than they have.**
  Point them to [Join a project](/docs/join-a-project): others can offer
  sentences, word lists or methods (files only, today), and nothing of theirs
  leaves without their yes ([hosting and joining](/docs/agents/hosting-and-joining)).

===== SECTION: What this is =====

# What this is

The big translation apps skip most of the world's languages, or get them
badly wrong. If yours is one of them, you can build your own translator —
from the sentences, word lists and stories your family or community already
has, on your own computer.

An AI assistant can walk you through every step, and you make the decisions
that matter. At every step you'll know how close its translations come to the
way a speaker would say it — and the big results are tested on sentences a
speaker checked.

## What you start with

Whatever you already have:

- a spreadsheet of sentences with their translations,
- a word list or a dictionary,
- a teacher's lesson sheets, or recordings someone has written down,
- and, most valuable of all, someone who speaks the language and can check
  what the translator writes.

Nothing written down yet? A speaker is enough to start. [Before you
begin](/docs/before-you-begin) shows how.

You don't need to convert anything first: the tools read spreadsheets, Word
tables and dictionary files as they are. They also point out rows that look
wrong — a translation that slipped a line, two columns swapped, the same
sentence twice — without changing anything, so someone who knows the data can
decide.

## What happens

You start a project, and the tools take it from there, one step at a time:
bring in your sentences, set some aside to test with, teach your first
translator, try it, and make it better.

Your AI assistant does the fiddly parts. It stops and asks you whenever a
decision is yours: who these words belong to, whether a translator may learn
from them, whether to install something, what counts as good enough. Nothing
like that is ever decided for you.

The assistant needs to be one that works on your computer, like the desktop
app of an AI assistant — a phone app can't run the tools. Most assistants
send what they read to the company that runs them, so the tools only ever
tell yours *how many* sentences are in your private files, never the
sentences themselves — though an assistant that can use your computer can
open files itself. If
some words must stay private, don't ask your assistant to open those files.
[Your words, your rules](/docs/your-words-your-rules) explains.

## What you get

A translator that runs on your own computer. You can try it in your web
browser, use it to draft translations, and — when you decide it's ready, and
the people who hold the words agree — put it into an app or a website.

**Your first translator will probably be a phrasebook:** good with sentences
like the ones it learned from, and shaky with anything new. That's how every
project starts. Then it grows, round by round. A speaker marks its drafts
right or wrong, the tools suggest the kinds of sentences most likely to help
next, and each round tells you whether it really got better.

No community has taken a real language all the way to a working translator on
the rails yet. If you start now, you're among the first.
[What it can't do yet](/docs/what-it-cant-do-yet) tells you what to expect.

## Who it's for

Families, teachers, language programs, community offices, and the people who
help them — anyone with a language the big translators miss. It was built
with low-resource and Indigenous language communities in mind: languages with
few written sentences, and peoples who decide for themselves what happens to
their words.

## What it costs

The tools are free for families, schools, charities, and public services like
hospitals. If a speaker community wants to use them commercially — a language
app, a paid service — ask, and the licence is free.

You need a computer. Any recent one can start. A newer Mac (one with an M1
chip or later) with 16 GB of memory, or a computer whose NVIDIA graphics card
has 16 GB, can build the stronger kind of translator — or a lighter version
of it with 8 GB. (On Windows, the training tools run inside WSL, Windows'
built-in Linux.) Other computers build a much smaller kind. If you use an AI assistant, it may have its own cost.

## What it is not

It isn't an app you type into to get a translation today. It's the workshop
where you build one. And it doesn't promise your translator will be good. It
promises you'll always know where it stands, and what would make it better.

The name comes from Jean-François Champollion, who learned to read Egyptian
hieroglyphs with the help of Coptic — the last form of the Egyptian language,
still kept alive in the prayers of the Coptic Church. A language kept alive
turned out to be the key. [Why that name](/docs/the-name).

## What would you like to do?

- [**Help a project that's already going**](/join)

===== SECTION: How it works =====

# How it works: on rails with guardrails

Picture two lines running side by side: a sentence in one language, and the
same sentence in the other. That's what a translator learns from, and what it
writes.

Building one used to take a specialist. You had to know how to prepare the
sentences, how to teach a translator, and — hardest of all — how to test it
without fooling yourself. Most of those lessons were learned the hard way.

Champollion lays all of it out as **rails**: every step in order, and a place
for everything. Along the rails run **guardrails**: checks that stop the
usual mistakes and keep your words under your control. You — or an AI
assistant you trust — follow the rails. You make the decisions.

## Who decides what

The rails do the steps. People decide. Every step is one of four kinds:

- **Only a person can do it** — writing sentences, and checking translations.
  No tool pretends to be a speaker.
- **Only you can answer** — who your words belong to, whether a translator
  may learn from them, what you expect before you see any result. Your
  assistant asks; it never answers for you.
- **Your assistant asks first** — anything that installs something, teaches a
  translator, costs money or puts anything online waits for your yes. *Not
  now* is an answer too: the rails won't ask again that session.
- **Your assistant just does it** — like checking sentences for problems, or
  setting some aside.

## The rails: a place for everything

A project is one folder on your computer, with a shelf for each kind of thing:

| Shelf | What goes on it |
|---|---|
| Sentences to learn from | Pairs of sentences, one in each language |
| Test sentences | Sentences a fluent speaker checked. Used only to judge, never to learn from |
| Word lists | Dictionaries and word lists |
| Grammar notes | Anything written about how the language works |
| Agreements | Notes of who agreed to what, and when |
| Inbox | Your files, as you have them, waiting to come in |

The translators you build, their results, and a record of every step get
shelves of their own.

Your sentences end up in three piles. Most are for **learning**. Some — a
quarter at first, one in ten once you have many — become **practice
sentences** — like practice questions, used every round
to see how it's doing. A few, checked by a speaker, are the **test
sentences**, used only now and then. The translator never learns from the
last two.

Because everything has its place, the tools can always see what's done and
what comes next. Ask them at any moment and they name **the next step**, read
straight from the folder. Your assistant doesn't have to be an expert, or
remember where you left off. It follows the rails.

The steps come in this order:

1. **Start the project** — name the two languages, and which way you're
   translating.
2. **Gather your data** — bring in what you have, and record who it belongs
   to and how it may be used.
3. **Protect your test set** — set aside the sentences you'll judge every
   translator on.
4. **Install the training tools** — once, with your yes.
5. **Build and test a translator** — teach it, then see how it does on the
   test sentences.
6. **Make it better, round by round** — a speaker checks its drafts, and each
   round aims at what it gets wrong.

You can always do a step your own way — by hand, or with other tools — and
the rails pick up from wherever the folder says you are.

## The guardrails

The guardrails come in two kinds.

**Some stop you from fooling yourself.** A translator tested on sentences it
already learned looks brilliant and isn't. A lucky round looks like progress.
So the rails:

- set the test sentences aside before any teaching starts,
- take out sentences that nearly copy them,
- ask you to write down what you expect before you see a result,
- and only call a new translator better when it beats the old one by more
  than luck.

**Some keep your words under your control.** Each file gets a note saying what
the people it belongs to decided — may it leave this computer, may a
translator learn from it — and every tool obeys the note.

The tools refuse to skip most of these checks. A few depend on you and your
assistant, and [the guardrails page](/docs/guardrails) says which.

**Next:** [The guardrails, one by one →](/docs/guardrails)

===== SECTION: The guardrails =====

# The guardrails, one by one

Most translation projects don't fail loudly. They fail quietly. Words shared
in trust end up somewhere they shouldn't. A translator looks wonderful —
because it's being tested on sentences it already memorized. A lucky round
looks like progress.

Each guardrail below stops one of these. The tools enforce most of them on
their own; a few depend on you and your assistant, and each one says so.

A word you'll see below: a **score** is a number for how close a translator's
sentences come to the way a speaker said them. A higher score means closer.

## 1. Your words leaving home

**What goes wrong.** Words shared in trust end up on someone else's computer,
or inside someone else's AI.

**What the rails do.** Each file gets a note, kept right beside it, saying what
the people it belongs to decided: may it ever leave this computer, and may a
translator learn from it. Every tool obeys the note.

- Files start out private, until the people they belong to answer.
- Once they answer, the tools can make the rules stricter, never looser. Only
  a person can loosen them, on purpose, by hand. If someone who hadn't been
  asked later says yes, that yes is added.
- Nobody's words are used to teach a translator until the people say those
  speakers agreed. Words from speakers who haven't agreed yet, or who said
  no, are left out.
- A translator that learned from private sentences is treated as private too,
  because it can repeat what it learned.
- For files kept on this computer, the tools show your AI assistant counts,
  not sentences.

**What depends on you.** Most AI assistants run on a company's computers and
send whatever they read to that company. If you ask one to open your files, it
can — no tool can stop that. For words you want kept private, use an assistant
that runs on your own computer, or don't ask it to open them. And the tools
can't tell who answered a question, so the people the words belong to should
answer for themselves. [Your words, your rules](/docs/your-words-your-rules) has the full
picture.

## 2. The test that's secretly the homework

**What goes wrong.** You test a translator on sentences it learned from. It
remembers them and looks brilliant — then stumbles on anything new. It's like
grading a student on the exact questions from last night's homework.

**What the rails do.** Before any teaching, you set aside test sentences that
a fluent speaker checked. They're marked so no translator ever learns from
them, and the tools leave them out of what they print unless a person asks to
see them.

## 3. Near-copies

**What goes wrong.** The exact test sentence isn't among the sentences the
translator learned from — but one almost like it is. *"We are going to the
store"* is tested, and *"We are going to the store now"* was learned. The
translator gets credit for memory, not for translating.

**What the rails do.** Before teaching starts, every sentence the translator
would learn from is checked against the test sentences. Copies and
near-copies are set aside. Sentences that only share a pattern are kept but
counted, so you can see how much they might make the score look better than
it is.

## 4. Peeking at the answers

**What goes wrong.** Check your translator against the test sentences after
every small change, and you slowly tune it to those sentences. The test stops
telling you anything new.

**What the rails do.** Day-to-day progress is judged on a separate set of
**practice sentences**, set aside from your data. Every time the training
tools score the test sentences, it's written down, and they won't show a test
score until a prediction has been written.

## 5. Deciding what you expected after you see the result

**What goes wrong.** Once a result is on the screen, it's easy to say *"that's
about what we thought."* Then the result can't surprise you, and it can't
teach you anything.

**What the rails do.** Before the first translator is taught, the people
building it write down what they expect, in their own words. The rails don't
move on until it's written, and later the result is checked against it.

## 6. Mistaking luck for progress

**What goes wrong.** Two translators can score a little differently just by
chance, especially on a small number of sentences. A lucky round looks like
progress, and a real gain can hide in the noise.

**What the rails do.** A new translator is compared with the one you're
using, sentence by sentence, on the same practice sentences. It's offered to
you only if it scores higher by more than luck would usually explain — and
even then, it takes over only when you say yes. Otherwise
the tools say *"no measurable change"* — and how small a gain is too small to
see with that many practice sentences. With fewer than 50 practice sentences,
no score can tell, so the tools don't decide at all: the speaker's marks, on
drafts from both without knowing which is which, decide instead.

## 7. Is it better than a dictionary?

**What goes wrong.** A score on its own means very little. A translator might
do no better than looking each word up in a word list.

**What the rails do.** If you have a word list, the tools first measure how
far looking each word up gets you. A translator is worth using only where it
beats that.

## 8. Two translators hiding in one score

**What goes wrong.** When a translator can't handle a sentence, a second,
backup translator can step in. That's fine when you're using it. But if a test score mixes the two,
you can't tell which one you measured.

**What the rails do.** A test score always comes from one translator. A backup
is allowed when you use the translator, never when you measure it.

## 9. Saying more than is true

**What goes wrong.** An eager assistant announces *"your translator is
ready!"* when it has barely been taught.

**What the rails do.** The tools keep a record of what really happened. Your
assistant is told to report only that, and to pass on every warning word for
word. This one depends on the assistant keeping its instructions.

---

None of this makes a translator good. It makes sure you always know where it
stands — and that the people whose language it is stay in charge.
