===== SECTION: What it can't do yet =====

# What it can't do yet

Your first translator will probably be a **phrasebook**. It will be good with
sentences like the ones it learned from, and shaky with anything new. That's
normal: every project starts there.

What moves it forward is more sentences — the right kinds, checked by someone
who speaks the language. Every round, the tools tell you whether it really got
better, and suggest what would help most next. This page tells you, plainly,
what to expect along the way.

## A working translator takes a lot of sentences

How many? We don't know yet for any real language. Here is what we do know.

We made up a practice language, so that a computer could check every answer:
about 2,000 words, perfectly regular grammar, clean data. A translator taught
on a laptop then translated new everyday sentences it had never seen, and a
computer checked whether each one meant exactly what the English meant:

- after 6,400 example sentences, **about 79 in 100** were exactly right;
- after 25,600, **about 96 in 100**.

Every sentence with a word it had never seen came out wrong — about a third of
its misses at 6,400 examples; the rest were grammar it hadn't learned yet.
That's the first thing to know: **a translator can't translate a word it
never learned.** So the tools point it out: when a sentence has a word your
translator never saw in its lessons, they say which word — that line is very
likely wrong, however fluent it reads.

A real language is much richer than our practice one: far more everyday
words, words with several meanings, grammar that marks things English leaves
unsaid. So these numbers are a floor, not an estimate. A real language will
need more sentences, and we don't yet know how many more. We are measuring it
now.

What that means in time: we haven't measured a real speaker's time yet. If
writing or checking a sentence took about a minute, 6,400 sentences would be
about a hundred hours. Shared across a family and a class, an hour or two a
week each adds up — and a small translator helps with your most-used phrases
long before then. [How many sentences does it take?](/docs/how-many-sentences)
goes into it.

## It can't promise a good translator — only that you'll know

A score measures how close the translator comes to the way a speaker said a
sentence. A good translation worded differently can score low, and a fluent
wrong one can score fairly high. That's why a speaker checking the drafts
matters more than any number.

A score also speaks only for sentences like the ones it was measured on, and
with only a few sentences it is rough — the tools show you a range, not a
single number. It can't tell you whether the *next* sentence the translator
writes will be right. A fluent speaker decides what is fit to use.

## Nobody has taken a real language all the way yet

We've walked every step of the rails many times, with made-up languages and
with many different AI assistants, from an empty folder to a translator you
can try in your browser. In our latest practice runs — AI assistants helping
a pretend family — more than half went wrong at some step. We fixed those
steps and are testing again.

No community has yet taken a real language all the way to a working
translator on the rails. If you start now, you're among the first.

## Some parts aren't ready

- **The step-by-step tools come with the next version.** Until then, these
  pages describe how they will work. [Before you begin](/docs/before-you-begin)
  is what you can do today.
- **Letting others test translators on your sentences** — without ever seeing
  them — works, but it isn't on the rails yet. Today it means following a
  longer manual.
- **Your computer matters.** A newer Mac (M1 or later) with 16 GB of memory,
  or a computer whose NVIDIA graphics card has 16 GB of its own, can build the
  stronger kind of translator; with 8 GB, a lighter version of it, which
  hasn't been tried on an 8 GB computer yet. On Windows, the training tools
  need WSL (Windows' built-in Linux). Other computers build a much smaller
  kind, which stayed far behind in our tests.
- **Rounds take the computer's time.** Most rounds carry on from the
  translator you're using rather than starting over, but with the stronger
  translator a round can still take hours, and only one translator learns at
  a time on a computer.
- **Keep sentences short.** The stronger translator reads only so much of a
  sentence — less if your language uses its own alphabet. The tools count
  any sentence that was too long and tell you, so you can split it.
- **Spelling isn't checked for you.** If people spell the language in
  different ways, agree on one way for the project before you begin.

## It can't stop every leak

For files kept on this computer — the default — the tools show your AI
assistant counts, not sentences. But an assistant that can use your computer
can open any file you can, asked or not, and most send what they read to the
company that runs them.
[Your words, your rules](/docs/your-words-your-rules) explains what to do.

## A translator isn't a living language

A translator can help a language program, a school or a family. The
language lives in its speakers, and in being used every day.
[Translation is not revitalization](/docs/network/perspectives/translation-is-not-revitalization)
says more.

---

These limits will change as the work does. When one does, this page changes
with it.

## Go deeper

- [The guardrails, one by one](/docs/guardrails) — how each check works.
- [The technical limits](/docs/network/honest-limitations) — what the
  measurements cover and don't, trust tiers on published scores, sealed-test
  custody, and why no per-sentence confidence is given.
- About the practice-language numbers: one run per size, so the spread
  between runs isn't measured. "Exactly right" is an automatic check of every
  part of the meaning — verb, tense, person, negation, subject, object and
  more — against the invented language's own grammar, not a person's
  judgement. The translator was a pretrained byte-level model fine-tuned on an
  Apple-silicon laptop. How long it trains changes the result a lot (the same
  model and 6,400 sentences scored about 27 in 100 with a quarter of the
  training), so these are not limits. At 6,400 sentences, about 9 in 100
  translations were fluent, used real words, and meant something else. The
  smaller model the tools use on other computers got about 6 in 100 right at
  6,400 sentences.
- The stronger translator reads at most 320 bytes of a sentence — about 100
  letters of syllabics, since accented letters and letters of other alphabets
  take two to four bytes each. Training counts the pairs past the limit before it cuts
  them, and a served translation says what it cut.

===== SECTION: Bring what you have =====

# Bring what you have

A translator learns from **pairs**: a sentence in one language, and the same
sentence in the other. This page is about bringing yours in — and about the
questions you'll be asked for each file, which matter more than anything else
on the rails.

## What the tools can read

Bring your files as you keep them. You don't need to convert anything.

| You have | The tools read |
|---|---|
| A spreadsheet of sentences and translations | Excel (`.xlsx`), LibreOffice (`.ods`), `.csv`, `.tsv` or plain text |
| A table in a Word document | The table's rows |
| A dictionary made in Toolbox or FieldWorks (programs many linguists use) | The words — and its example sentences, as pairs |
| Recordings written down in ELAN (a program for transcribing recordings) | The written-down lines and their translations, as pairs |
| A word list | Each word and its translation |
| Notes about the grammar | Kept in their own place, for people and tools to refer to |
| Scripture | Only if you ask, and no translator learns from it until the people who hold it say so |

Your files are read where they are. If a spreadsheet's columns don't say which
language is which, the tools ask you — they never guess from the contents.

The tools also look for rows that seem wrong — a translation that slipped down
a line, two columns swapped, a translation copied from the other side, the
same pair twice, a translation far longer or shorter than usual — and tell
you which rows, by number. They never change or remove anything; someone who
knows the data decides.

## The tools count. They don't read your words out to anyone.

When a file comes in, the tools tell you how many pairs they found and which
columns they used. That's all your AI assistant is shown: counts and column
names, never the sentences themselves.

## The questions for each file

Before anything learns from a file, the rails ask the people who hold it:

- **Who does it belong to?** In your own words — a family, a teacher, a
  community office.
- **Whose words are in it?** The people who said or wrote the sentences. A
  grandmother's notebooks hold her words, even if her grandson typed them.
- **Have they agreed to their use?** *Yes*, *not yet*, or *some said no*.
  The rails keep asking until this is answered. Words from people who haven't
  agreed yet, or who said no, are never used to teach a translator.
- **May a translator learn from it?**
- **May it ever leave this computer?** Files start out private — kept on this
  computer — until you answer.

The answers are written in a small note beside the file, and every tool obeys
it. After your first answer, the tools can only make the rules stricter, never
looser. The one exception: a speaker who hadn't been asked yet can still say
yes.

Your assistant asks these questions; it must never answer them for you. If you
don't know yet — say, you still need to ask an aunt — say *not yet*. The rails
set that file aside and carry on, and ask again later, gently.

## What you'll see

In our practice run of the tools — an illustration with invented sentences —
a family brought in four files: <WalkFact of="trainingFiles.0.pairs" />
sentence pairs from a grandfather's spreadsheet, <WalkFact of="trainingFiles.1.pairs" />
from an aunt's, a word list of <WalkFact of="lexicon.pairs" /> words, and
<WalkFact of="test.pairs" /> sentences a speaker had checked, for testing. Each
time, the assistant reported the count, and then asked who the file belonged
to and whether a translator could learn from it.

## Sentences from other places

If you use sentences you didn't write — from a book, a website, a published
collection — they come with their own rules. Some may be read but not shared;
some may not be used to teach anything. Bring them in the same way, and answer
the questions honestly for them too: the tools will hold them to your answer.
When a collection's licence is unusual or unclear, the tools won't send it to
an outside AI service until its owners have said yes.

===== SECTION: Set aside your test sentences =====

# Set aside your test sentences

Before any translator learns anything, you set aside a few sentences to test
it with. This is the most important step on the rails. Every result you'll
ever see is measured on these sentences — so if they're wrong, every result is
wrong.

## Why it matters

Imagine testing a student with the exact questions from their homework. They'd
look brilliant, and you'd learn nothing about what they can really do. A
translator is the same. Tested on sentences it learned from, it simply
remembers them.

So the test sentences are kept apart: no translator ever learns from them, and
they're used only to judge.

## Choosing good test sentences

- **Checked by a fluent speaker.** Each sentence and its translation should be
  right, in the way your community says it.
- **Real sentences you'd want translated.** Everyday things you'd say at home,
  write in a note, or teach in a class — the kinds of sentences the translator
  is for.
- **A mix.** Questions, statements, requests; short ones and longer ones.
- **Not copied from the sentences you'll teach with.** Write them fresh, or
  take them from a separate source.
- **Spelled the same way as the rest.** Agree on one way to spell the
  language before you start.
- **As many as your speaker can check.** A few dozen is a start; with so few,
  every result is rough, and the tools show you a wide range instead of a
  single number. A few hundred let you see smaller differences.

## How the rails protect them

You put them in their own place — the test shelf — and the tools mark them:

- private: kept on this computer, unless the people who hold them decide
  otherwise,
- never to be learned from,
- kept out of what the tools print.

Then, before teaching starts, every sentence the translator would learn from
is checked against the test sentences. Copies and near-copies are set aside,
so the translator can't get credit for memory.

And every time the training tools score the test sentences, it's written
down. Day to
day, progress is judged on a separate set of **practice sentences**, so the
test sentences stay fresh for the moments that matter.

## What you'll see

In the recorded walk — an illustration with invented sentences — the family
set aside <WalkFact of="test.pairs" /> checked sentences. When the tools checked
the other sentences against them, they found that <WalkFact of="twins.n" /> of them, about <WalkFact of="twins.pct" />
in 100, had a near-copy among the sentences the family meant to teach with.
Those near-copies were set aside before any teaching began. Without that step,
the first score would have looked better than it was.

## Sharing a test set later

Your test sentences can stay on your computer forever — that's the default.
If you ever want others to be able to measure against them, the tools can
register the set at one of four levels:

- **Kept here** — never registered; nothing leaves this computer.
- **Listed privately** — only a description of the set is shared, never the
  sentences. Results can be published without anyone seeing the data.
- **Listed publicly** — a description, plus a pointer to where the set is
  already published. Only for sets whose licence allows it. Champollion never
  hosts the sentences.
- **Sealed** — locked on your computer with a key, so others can try their
  translators on it without ever seeing it.

[Host a sealed test](/docs/host-a-sealed-test) explains the last one.

===== SECTION: Your first translator =====

# Your first translator

This is the exciting part: the first time a translator learns from your
sentences, and you try it. It's also where the rails are most careful, because
the first result is the one people remember.

## Before teaching starts

Your assistant walks through these in order. Most it simply does; it stops
and asks you where a step is yours.

1. **Install the training tools** — once, and only with your yes. They're
   downloaded to your computer.
2. **Gather the sentences into one file** — the tools combine your files,
   keep the strictest of their rules, and leave out exact repeats. Files that
   no translator may learn from are moved aside, not deleted.
3. **Check against the test sentences** — copies and near-copies of your test
   sentences are set aside.
4. **Write down what you expect** — before any result exists, in your own
   words. *"A phrasebook at best"* is a perfectly good prediction. The rails
   won't move on until it's written.
5. **Set aside practice sentences** — a quarter of your sentences while you
   have fewer than 200, then 50, then one in ten once that's more, held back so the translator can be checked as it learns without touching
   the test sentences.
6. **Measure the dictionary** — if you brought a word list, the tools first
   see how far simply looking each word up gets you. Your translator is worth
   using only where it beats that.

## Teaching

Then the translator learns. It runs on your computer and nothing is sent
anywhere. The tools look at your computer's memory and pick what it can
handle: on a newer Mac, or with an NVIDIA graphics card, the stronger kind of
translator (or a lighter version of it, with less memory); on other
computers, a much smaller one. Only one translator learns at a time on a
computer.

It can take a while — minutes for a small one, a few hours for the stronger
kind. It watches itself: if it shows no sign of life at the start, stops
making progress, or runs past a day, it stops and says why. Nothing runs
forever.

## The first result

When it's done, the translator is tested on your test sentences, and you see
a **score**: a number out of 100 for how close its translations come to the
way your speaker said them. Beside it, the tools show a range — how sure they
are — and every warning that applies, word for word.

Then you can try it yourself, in your web browser, with your own sentences.

## What you'll see

In our practice run of the tools — made-up sentences, and a pretend
translator so the run takes seconds — the family predicted *"a phrasebook at
best"*. Then:

- Looking words up in their word list scored about <WalkFact of="floor.score" round />
  out of 100 on <WalkFact of="floor.devSentences" /> practice sentences.
- The first translator scored about <WalkFact of="devModel.score" round /> on
  the same practice sentences — **below the word list.**
- The tools said so plainly, and warned that <WalkFact of="smallSample.n" />
  practice sentences is too few to show anything but big differences.
- The prediction held, and the grandfather recorded it.

That's a real lesson, not a failure. With a few dozen sentences, a word list
often wins at first. The rails make sure you *know* that, instead of being
told it's ready — and the rounds that follow are how you pass it.

## When it's a phrasebook

It almost always is, at first: good with sentences like the ones it learned
from, and shaky with anything new. It can still be useful — for drafts that a
speaker corrects, or for phrases you use again and again. And it's the start
of the rounds that make it better.

  dictionary floor and predictions, exactly.
- [Reading the numbers](/docs/reading-the-numbers) — every number, in plain
  words.

===== SECTION: Make it better, round by round =====

# Make it better, round by round

Your first translator is a beginning, not an end. From here it grows in
**rounds**. Each round, a speaker checks what it writes, you add the sentences
that would help most, and it learns again. At the end of every round you get
a short report: what changed, how sure the tools are, and what to do next.

This is the heart of the rails. It's also where a speaker's time does the most
good.

## Before the first round: how much time?

The rails start by asking how much time the speaker can give — a week, and in
all. Each round is sized to that. Once a few rounds show a trend, the rails
tell you plainly what that time looks like it can buy, including when it
looks like too little. They never push for more. The speaker's time is theirs.

## One round

1. **A wish list.** The tools look at what the translator gets wrong and make
   a printable sheet of what would help most: words it has never seen — with
   two or three sentences asked for each, since a word met only once is
   rarely learned — and the kinds of sentences it stumbles on. A quarter of the sheet stays open, so you
   still write what *you* need. Use it as much or as little as you like.
2. **Your sentences.** Write 20 or more sentences you'd really want
   translated — things you'd say at home, write in a note, or teach in a
   class. As many as the speaker can check this week.
3. **The translator drafts them.** It writes a translation of each onto a
   sheet for the speaker. While there are few practice sentences, some rows
   have no draft — one in two until there are 50 practice sentences, then one
   in four until there are 200. The speaker writes those, and they become new
   practice sentences (never learned from).
4. **The speaker checks.** For each draft: **Y** if it's right; **N** if it's
   wrong, and then how it should be said; **?** if unsure. Open it in a
   spreadsheet, or print it and type the marks in afterwards.

   From the second round, about one row in ten comes back from an earlier
   sheet, on purpose — the sheet says so at the top, but not which rows.
   Mark them fresh, as if new. How often the marks agree tells everyone how
   far they can be trusted. Those rows cost a few seconds each, and they
   never count toward the round's result.
5. **The tools read the marks.** They count how many drafts were right. The
   fixes, and the drafts marked right, become new sentences to learn from —
   after you've said who they belong to, like any file.
6. **The report.** See below.
7. **Learn again.** With your yes, the translator learns from everything so
   far — usually carrying on from the one you're using, so a round takes less
   time than the first teaching did. The new one is compared with the one
   you're using, sentence by sentence, on the same practice sentences. Only
   if it's better by more than luck do the rails offer it to you — and it
   takes over only when you say yes. Otherwise the one you're using stays,
   and the next round begins. With fewer than 50 practice
   sentences, no score can tell which is better — so the tools don't guess.
   The one you're using stays, and the speaker decides instead (see below).

## The round report

Each report starts with the progress, then the checks, then what to do:

- **The speaker's share of drafts marked right** — the number that matters
  most — with a range showing how sure the tools are.
- **The practice score** — a number out of 100 for how close the translator
  comes, on practice sentences it never learned from — and whether the new
  translator really beat the old one.
- **A check that it isn't just memorizing** — whether the gains on practice
  sentences also show up on new sentences.
- **How far the marks can be trusted** — once ten rows shown again have been
  marked: how often the speaker marked them the same way, and whether drafts
  once marked wrong are now being marked right more often, which can happen
  as anyone grows used to a translator. That's no one's fault, and it's worth
  knowing.
- **How far to "working"** — once the rise is real, a range for how many more
  sentences and hours it looks like, each time your sentences double. The
  range also takes in how far the speaker's marks can be trusted.
- **Two to four things to do next** — like *write sentences with these words*,
  *mark this sheet*, *try the stronger translator*, or *ask for help through
  Join a project*.

Your assistant is told to relay all of it with every number's meaning, to
celebrate only gains the tools measured, and to say *"no measurable change"*
plainly when that's the result. A round with no measurable change still
counts: the translator you're using stays, and you know where you stand.

## The speaker checks without knowing which is which

Two moments get a blind check on your own sentences:

- **After you put a new translator to use**, the next sheet mixes its drafts with
  drafts from the one it replaced — picked at random, not labelled. A rise
  counts as real progress only when the speaker's own marks agree.
- **When the practice sentences can't decide** — there are fewer than 50, or
  the round showed no measurable change — half of the next sheet's drafts
  come from the new translator. If the speaker clearly prefers it, the rails
  offer to put it to use (you still say yes), and the report says it was
  chosen on the speaker's marks.

Either way, the speaker marks every draft the same way, without knowing which
translator wrote it.

## When the rounds stop moving

Two rounds in a row with no rise you can see doesn't mean the rounds stopped
helping. Once a translator is fairly good, a round may add less than your
practice sentences can show. The report says so plainly — it can't tell a
small gain from none — and points at the faster ways forward: a stronger
translator, or more sentences of the kinds it gets wrong.

If you started with the small kind of translator, your computer can teach the
stronger kind, and two rounds in a row since you last changed translators
show no measurable gain, the rails offer to switch. (Rounds with too few
practice sentences to tell don't count.) It's a bigger download and takes
longer to teach, so the rails ask: *yes*, or *not now*. If you say yes, it
learns from everything you have, and it's offered to you only if it's
measurably better — you still say yes before it takes over.

## People who haven't agreed yet

If some of your sentences come from people who haven't agreed yet, the rails
leave those aside and carry on. Each session, they ask once, gently, whether
everyone has agreed. When the answer is yes, those sentences join the next
round.

**Next:** [How many sentences does it take? →](/docs/how-many-sentences)

===== SECTION: How many sentences does it take? =====

# How many sentences does it take?

It's the first question everyone asks, and the honest answer has two parts:
**more than most people expect** — and **your own rounds will tell you.**

## What we know

We made up a practice language, so a computer could check every answer:
about 2,000 words, perfectly regular grammar, clean data. A translator taught
on a laptop got the exact meaning of new everyday sentences right:

- about **79 in 100** after **6,400** example sentences,
- about **96 in 100** after **25,600**.

Every sentence with a word it had never seen came out wrong — though those
were only about a third of its misses at 6,400 examples. The rest were
grammar it hadn't learned yet.

## What we don't know

How many *your* language needs. A real language has far more everyday words
than our practice one, words with several meanings, and grammar that marks
things English leaves unsaid. So the counts above are a floor: a real language
will need more, and we don't yet know how much more. We're measuring it.

Anyone who gives you a single number for your language, today, is guessing.

## How to estimate yours

Your rounds are the best estimate there is. Once a few rounds — with a better
translator put to use along the way, confirmed by the speaker's blind check —
show a real rise in the speaker's marks, each round report gives a range for
how many more sentences, and how many hours of a speaker's time, it looks
like it would take to reach a translator that gets most new sentences right —
based on how much each doubling of your sentences has helped so far. The
projection updates every round, and it says plainly when the time you have
looks like too little.

## Time

We haven't measured a real speaker's time yet. As a rough guide: if writing
or checking a sentence took about a minute, 6,400 sentences would be about a
hundred hours of a speaker's time — and a real language will need more. That
can sound like a lot. Shared among a family, a class or a community, a couple
of hours a week each adds up — and [other people can help](/docs/join-a-project).

## Make every sentence count

The number of sentences matters less than *which* sentences:

- **Use real sentences.** Things your family actually wants to say beat
  made-up drills. On our practice language, everyday sentences taught more
  than sentences picked to pack in as many new words as possible: after
  3,200 of them, 53 in 100 new sentences came out with the exact meaning
  right, against 39 in 100 — for about the same speaker time.
- **A few sentences for each word.** A word the translator meets only once is
  rarely learned. The rails' wish list names words it has never seen; give
  each one two or three sentences, each saying something different. Fewer
  words, each in a few sentences, teach more than many words once.
- **Aim at the mistakes.** Sentences like the ones it gets wrong teach more
  than random ones. The wish list suggests those too.
- **Keep them short and varied.** Short sentences, many kinds — questions,
  requests, stories.
- **Corrections are gold.** When a speaker marks a draft wrong and writes how
  it should be said, that's exactly where the translator went wrong.

**Next:** [Put it to work →](/docs/put-it-to-work)

===== SECTION: Put it to work =====

# Put it to work

A translator is for using. Here are the ways to use yours, from the simplest
to the biggest — and the one rule that runs through all of them: **the people
who hold the words decide what leaves your computer.**

## Try it in your browser

The quickest way. The tools start your translator on your computer and give
you a page to open in your web browser. Type a sentence, see the translation.
Nothing leaves your computer. If your sentence has a word the translator never
saw in its lessons, the page says which — that line is very likely wrong,
however fluent it reads.

If your translator learned from private sentences, it can repeat them — so
the rails' try tool won't pass its translations to your AI assistant (that
would send them to the assistant's company). It gives you the page's address
instead, and you look there yourself. An assistant that can run commands on
your computer could still ask the translator directly, so ask it not to.

## Translate documents

Give the tools a file of sentences, and they translate every line into a new
file, on your computer, using the settings the translator was tested with.
The new file is held to the same rules as the sentences the translator
learned from.

## Run it as a service

The tools can run your translator as a small service on your computer, so
other programs can ask it for translations. By default, only programs on the
same computer can reach it, and it can require a password.

Making it reachable from other computers is a bigger step. For a translator
that learned from private sentences, the tools refuse until you name who,
among the people who hold the words, agreed — and that is written down.

## Connect it to an app

If you're building an app, the tools can connect your translator to it, so the
app's words are translated by your translator. The same rule applies: a
translator that learned from private sentences connects only once you've
named who agreed.

## On other computers and phones

Your translator lives on the computer that built it. For a school or an office
to use it from other computers or phones, it has to be reachable from them —
by running it as a service on your network, or inside an app. Both are bigger
steps, and for a translator that learned from private sentences, both wait for
the people who hold the words to agree. If you'd like a hand with this part,
[let's talk](/docs/getting-help).

## Translate an app or website's words

For translating the buttons, menus and pages of an app or website — and
keeping them up to date as the original changes —
[Translate an app or website](/docs/translate-an-app-or-website) has the whole
story.

## In daily use: a speaker has the last word

However good the scores, a person who speaks the language should read anything
before it's published. A good way to work is drafts: the translator writes, a
speaker corrects. Every correction is also a gift to the next round — it's
exactly where the translator went wrong.

When something wrong does get out, fix it in the open and say what changed.
Mistakes caught and owned build more trust than a translator that claims to
be perfect.

**Next:** [Your words, your rules →](/docs/your-words-your-rules)

===== SECTION: Your words, your rules =====

# Your words, your rules

Language shared in trust has too often been recorded, collected or used to
train someone else's technology — and then held by outsiders, while the
people whose language it is had to ask permission for their own words. The
rails are built so that doesn't happen here.

The rule is simple: **the people who hold the words decide what happens to
them.** The tools write those decisions down, and obey them.

## Where your words go

By default, nowhere. Your files stay on your computer. The tools bring them in
where they are, and show your AI assistant only counts and column names.

[Where your data goes](/your-data) shows every case side by side: your
files, what your assistant is told, a translator's output, a test set you
choose to register, and the few things that do leave your computer — like the
language's code, when the tools look up its public information card.

## The note beside every file

Each file gets a small note, written by the tools from your answers:

- who it belongs to, and whose words are in it;
- whether those people have agreed — *yes*, *not yet*, or *some said no*;
- whether a translator may learn from it;
- whether it may ever leave this computer.

Every tool reads the note and obeys it — including offering a file to someone
else's project, which refuses a private file, or one whose speakers haven't
all agreed. Files start out private. After the
first answer, the tools can only make the rules stricter — except to record a
*yes* from someone who hadn't been asked yet. Loosening a rule is something
the people who hold the words do by hand, on purpose.

## What's built from your words is yours

A translator learns from your sentences, so it carries your rules with it:

- A translator that learned from private sentences is treated as private too,
  because it can repeat what it learned. Its translations stay on your
  computer unless the people who hold the words agree, and say who agreed.
- Champollion claims no ownership of any translator, word list, or anything
  else built from a community's words — and wants none. Writing the tools
  doesn't make us owners of what you build with them.
- Scores can be shared without the sentences. You can publish how well a
  translator did, and keep every sentence private.

## Other people's collections

If you use sentences someone else published, their rules come too:

- **When the tools send sentences out, they follow the licence.** A collection
  whose licence is unusual or unclear is never interpreted on its owners'
  behalf: it isn't sent until its owners say what's allowed. Whether your own
  use is commercial is something no tool can check — that part is yours.
- **Sending sentences to an outside AI is a decision.** Testing an AI model
  means sending it sentences. Collections with a plain non-commercial licence
  go only to services that promise not to learn from what they're sent.
  Collections with unclear terms aren't sent at all until their owners agree.
  Sealed sets never leave the computer that holds them.
- **Champollion doesn't host collections.** The tools point to where a
  collection is published, and fetch it from there. Two exceptions: files
  someone offers through [Join a project](/docs/join-a-project) are stored on
  Champollion's project storage, and a published score for an openly
  licensed test set can include its sentences.

## What no tool can stop

The tools are careful, but some things are up to people:

- **Your AI assistant can open a file if you ask it to.** Most assistants send
  what they read to the company that runs them. For words you want kept
  private, use an assistant that runs on your own computer, or don't ask it to
  open them.
- **Anyone can paste words into a chat.** The tools can't see that happening.
- **The tools can't tell who answered.** When the rails ask who holds a file,
  or whether a speaker agreed, the right person should answer for themselves.

## Our part

We build so that communities can own and control their language data, and
anything made from it. Whether we succeed is for communities to judge — we're
working toward it, and we don't claim we've reached it.

We never name a community, nation or organization as a partner, or as holding
a key, without its consent. If you find your community named here without
that consent, tell us, and we'll remove it.

## Objections and takedowns

If something here is wrong, disrespectful, or uses your community's words or
name in a way you didn't agree to, we want to hear it — in your own words. You
don't need an account.

- **Write to** [info@champollion.dev](mailto:info@champollion.dev), or use
  the site guide's message form (the chat panel → *Send a message*). To ask
  for something to be removed, put **Takedown** in the subject, or choose
  *Takedown* in the form.
- **Our default is to act.** We host almost no one's sentences, so most
  removals are a listing, a citation or a field on a page — and those we take
  down quickly.
- **We say what we did.** If we can't do what you ask, we say why, and who
  decides.
- **Security problems:** [security@champollion.dev](mailto:security@champollion.dev).

**Next:** [Working with speakers →](/docs/working-with-speakers)

===== SECTION: Working with speakers =====

# Working with speakers

The most valuable part of any translator project isn't the computer. It's the
people who speak the language — who write sentences, check drafts, and say
*"no, we'd say it like this."* If that's you, this page is about you, and for
the people working beside you.

## Ask each person

Every sentence came from someone. Before a translator learns from anyone's
words, ask them — or, if that isn't possible, ask the people who decide for
them.

- **Ask in plain words** what the sentences will be used for, who will see
  them, and that they can say no.
- **Write it down.** The rails keep a place for agreements: who agreed to
  what, and when. The note beside each file records whether the speakers
  agreed — *yes*, *not yet*, or *some said no* — and the tools obey it.
- **"Not yet" is a fine answer.** The rails set those sentences aside and
  carry on, and ask again later.
- **When someone has passed on**, their words are a question for their family
  and community, never something to assume.
- **People can change their minds.** Make it easy for them to.

## Respect their time

Checking translations is real work. The rails ask how much time a speaker can
give before planning anything, size each round to it, and never push for
more. If the time looks like too little to reach your goal, they say so
honestly, so you can decide together — or find more hands through
[Join a project](/docs/join-a-project).

Short sessions work better than long ones. Checking gets harder when you're
tired, and a tired *"yes"* teaches the translator the wrong thing. Marking a
draft **?** — *not sure* — is always allowed.

## Credit, and payment

- **Credit people the way they want** — by name, by family, by community, or
  not at all. Ask.
- **Paying speakers for their time is right**, and in your project it's for
  the people leading it to decide. Champollion takes no share of anything a
  community earns, and anything a sponsor gives passes straight through.

## Sacred and restricted words

Some words aren't for everyone: ceremonial language, sacred stories, things
only certain people may say, or say at certain times. **Leave them out.** A
translator can repeat what it learned, to anyone, at any time — so if words
shouldn't travel, they shouldn't be taught.

When you're not sure, ask the people who would know, and leave them out until
you are. Enthusiastic agreement is the bar, not the absence of an objection.

## Choose how to spell

If people write the language in different ways, the translator learns a
muddle. Before you begin, agree on one way to spell it for the project — the
system a school uses, or a community's standard — and say which dialect the
sentences come from. The tools don't check spelling for you yet, so this is a
human decision, made once and written down.

## Checking drafts

When the rails hand a speaker a sheet of drafts:

- **Y** — the draft is right, the way you'd say it.
- **N** — it's wrong. Then write how you *would* say it. That correction is
  the most useful sentence there is: it's exactly where the translator went
  wrong.
- **?** — not sure. That's fine.

A draft can be right and still sound different from how you'd say it. Mark
what's right as right; write a better way if you have one.

From the second round, a few rows come back from earlier sheets on purpose —
the sheet says so, but not which. Mark them fresh, as if new. Nobody marks
perfectly the same twice, and that's fine: how often the marks agree just
tells everyone how far the results can be trusted.

===== SECTION: Reading the numbers =====

# Reading the numbers

The rails show you numbers at every step. Each one is only useful if you know
three things about it: **what it measures**, **out of what**, and **on which
sentences**. The tools say all three, and your assistant is told to. This page
explains each kind.

## The speaker's share of drafts marked right

**The number that matters most.** Each round, a speaker marks the translator's
drafts right or wrong. *"31 of 40 drafts marked right"* means just what it
says: on the 40 sentences your family wanted translated this round, the
speaker judged 31 right.

Nothing a computer measures beats a speaker's judgement. But it depends on the
sentences: an easy week and a hard week can give different numbers with the
same translator. That's why the tools also measure the same way each time, on
the same sentences — the score.

## The score, out of 100

A **score** is a number from 0 to 100 for how close the translator's sentences
come to the way a speaker wrote the same sentences. It counts matching
letters and words, and gives partial credit: a translation that's nearly
right scores higher than one that's way off. 100 means identical.

Two things to know:

- **It measures closeness, not correctness.** A good translation worded
  differently from the speaker's can score low. A fluent translation that
  means something else can score fairly high. That's why a speaker's check
  matters more.
- **It's not a percentage of sentences right.** A score of 60 doesn't mean
  60 in 100 sentences were right.

For the curious: this score is called **chrF++**, and it's the field's usual
way to compare translators. The tools also report others beside it.

## Ranges

Most numbers come with a **range**, like *14–22*. That's not two results. It's
how sure the tools are: the real value is very likely somewhere in there. With
a few sentences, the range is wide. With many, it narrows.

When two ranges overlap a lot, the two translators may really be the same.

## Which sentences

A number always says which sentences it was measured on:

- **Test sentences** — the ones a speaker checked and the translator never
  learned from. Used for the results that matter, and only now and then.
- **Practice sentences** — set aside from your data, and also never learned
  from. Used to judge each round, so the test sentences stay fresh.
- **Your round's sentences** — the ones your family wanted translated; the
  speaker's marks are on these.

A number measured on sentences the translator learned from would mean nothing,
so the rails never show you one as a result.

## "No measurable change"

This doesn't mean nothing changed. It means any change was too small to tell
apart from luck, with the number of practice sentences you have. The tools say
how big a change they *could* have seen. More practice sentences let them see
smaller changes — which is why, while the practice set is small, some rows of
each round's sheet are left for the speaker to write.

## "Too few practice sentences to tell"

With fewer than 50 practice sentences, no score can reliably say which of two
translators is better. On our practice language, with 23 practice sentences,
the careful rule called two nearly equal translators different 9 times in
100 — and noticed a real gain of about 6 points out of 100 only 21 times in
100. With 50, those were 4 and 96. So below 50, the tools don't call it. The one you're using stays, and the speaker's marks on
the next sheet decide.

## The dictionary floor

If you brought a word list, you'll see a score for *just looking each word
up*. It's the floor: a translator is worth using only where it scores above
it. With very few sentences, a first translator can fall below it. That's
worth knowing, not worth hiding.

## A number you'll see on our pages: "meaning right"

When we talk about our made-up practice language, you'll see *"79 in 100
exactly right"*. That one is a share of sentences: a computer checked every
part of each translation's meaning against the made-up language's own grammar.
It's only possible on a language we invented, where the right answer is known
exactly. On a real language, the nearest thing is a speaker's marks.

===== SECTION: Getting help =====

# Getting help

**Having trouble, or want help with your project? Let's talk.**
Write to [info@champollion.dev](mailto:info@champollion.dev?subject=Help%20with%20a%20language%20project).

You never need us to build a translator: the rails are made so that you, or
an AI assistant you trust, can go all the way on your own. But some projects
go faster, or feel safer, with people beside you.

## What help can look like

Whatever your project needs, worked out with you:

- **Getting set up** — on your computers, the way your community wants.
- **Organising your data** — bringing scattered files together, choosing a
  spelling system, setting aside good test sentences.
- **Teaching and training** — showing your team how the rails work, so you
  can carry on without us.
- **Building with you** — doing some of the technical work, under your
  direction.
- **Running things for you** — if your community asks, and only if it
  chooses to.

There's no price list: we work out what makes sense with each community, for
what it needs.

## Who we are

Champollion is a non-Indigenous project. We work in a service role, and only
by consent: your community decides what happens to its language, its data and
anything built from it. We take no share of anything a community earns from
its own language.

## Other ways to get help

- **[Join a project](/docs/join-a-project)** — list your project so other
  people can offer sentences, word lists or methods.
- **Your AI assistant** — it can explain any step. Ask it *"why does this step
  matter?"* and it will tell you what the rails say.

**Next:** [Join a project →](/docs/join-a-project)

===== SECTION: Join a project =====

# Join a project

A translator for a language with few written sentences needs many hands.
**Join a project** is how they find each other: people building a translator
list their project, say what would help, and others offer it.

## If you want to help

Browse the projects on the [Join a project](/join) page. Each one shows the
two languages, what the project is for, and what its holders are asking for —
sentences on certain topics, a word list, a method to try.

When you offer something:

- **You send it to the project, not to the public.** Your file is uploaded to
  Champollion's project storage, where only you, that project's holders, and
  the people who run that storage can open it.
- **It's held by you both.** You submitted it; they decide whether to take
  it. When they accept it, a note records who offered it, who accepted it,
  and what was agreed.
- **They see who you are.** The project's holders see the name and email you
  offered under, so they can reach you. The public page never shows an email.
- **They can say no.** A project may decline an offer.
- **You can withdraw it** before they've accepted it. Withdrawing (or their
  declining) changes the offer's status but doesn't delete the file, and the
  project's holders can still open it — so offer only what you're content for
  them to keep.
- **Its note comes first.** The tools won't offer a file marked private, or
  one whose speakers haven't all agreed — only its holders can change that.

What you won't get from a project: its sentences. Nothing of theirs is sent
to you without their yes.

## If you're building a translator

You can list your project once it's started on the rails. You'll say:

- the two languages, and what the translator is for,
- the name you want shown — never your email,
- what would help most.

Every listing gets a short review before it appears, so the page stays
trustworthy. When someone offers something, you decide: accept it, and it
arrives in your project's inbox with a note naming both of you, ready to bring
in like any file — or decline it.

## What can be offered today

Files: sentences, word lists, and ways of translating to try. Helping in other ways —
checking drafts from afar, or lending computer power — is not part of it yet.

When no projects are listed yet, the page says so honestly.

**Next:** [Translate an app or website →](/docs/translate-an-app-or-website)

===== SECTION: Host a sealed test =====

# Host a sealed test

Sometimes the best translator for your language will come from someone else —
a researcher, a student, a company. A **sealed test** lets them prove it on
*your* sentences, without ever seeing those sentences.

## How it works

Your test sentences are locked with a key, on your computer. People who want
to compete send in their translators. Your computer runs each one on the
locked sentences, and only the scores come out — never the sentences, and
never the translations.

So the test stays a real test: nobody can study it or tune to it, because
nobody can read it.

## What you decide

You set the terms, before anyone competes:

- **What counts as good enough** to win.
- **What happens to a winning method:**
  - **it becomes yours** — it passes to you, the people who hold the test;
  - **its maker keeps it** — you score it, and keep at most a locked copy for
    checking;
  - **its maker keeps it, but shares it with everyone** — they must publish it
    openly.
- **Whether there's a prize** at all, and who funds it. Champollion takes no
  share of any prize.

## What exists today

The tools for sealed tests work: locking a set, running submitted
translators on a computer cut off from the internet, and publishing only
scores. But this is **not on the rails yet** — today it means following a
longer manual, not answering an assistant's questions step by step.

Who holds the key today: whoever locks the set. No community has yet named
people to hold the key together, and Champollion holds no part of any key.

Open sealed tests, when there are any, are listed on the
[shared tasks](/shared-tasks) page.

**Back to the start:** [What this is →](/docs/what-is-champollion)

===== SECTION: Translate an app or website =====

# Translate an app or website

Apps and websites keep their words — buttons, menus, messages, pages — in
files, one per language. Champollion can fill in your language's file for
you, and keep it up to date whenever the original changes. One command does
it:

```bash
npx champollion sync
```

It finds your app's language files, translates only what's missing or
changed, checks every translation before writing it, and leaves the rest
alone.

## Which translator does the work

You choose, for each language:

- **Your own translator**, built on the rails — the tools connect it to your
  app. If it learned from private sentences, it connects only once you've
  named who, among the people who hold the words, agreed.
- **An AI model or a translation service** — for languages they already
  handle well. These send your app's words to the company that runs them, so
  use them for text that is fine to share.
- **Your own service**, at an address you give.

## What it takes care of

- **Only what changed.** It remembers what it translated before, so you never
  pay twice for the same sentence.
- **Checks before writing.** Empty answers, the original copied back, words
  repeating in a loop, text much longer than it should be, missing pieces, or
  the wrong alphabet are caught and refused. These checks catch broken output,
  not wrong meaning — a speaker still has the last word.
- **Your files, your format.** JSON, YAML, TOML and Markdown pages, and the
  common app and website frameworks.

## Who may use it

Free for noncommercial use — a school's app, a community website, a public
service. A business's product is not covered by the free licence; if a speaker
community wants to use it commercially, ask, and the licence is free.
[Who may use this](/docs/getting-started/who-may-use-this) has the details.
